gadget-service: improve logging of headless gadget instances

This changes the output format of gadget logs to JSON and adds the fields
"instanceID", "instanceName" and "gadget" to make them easier to digest for
existing postprocessing pipelines. This doesn't change the way the non-gadget
logging is handled, so that will still be in plain-text and should probably
be adjusted later on as well.

github: Fix release notes to add all other changes.

github actions: disable some cron jobs on forks

Before this patch, forks would run daily github actions to check the
links, check the artifact hub tags and run the scorecard analysis.

Most of the time, forks are just there to make pull requests. The main
branch is unused and becomes stale. It is a waste of resources to run
daily checks on it.

This patch disables these 3 cron jobs. Other cron jobs are left
unchanged because they are already disabled by default (unless the fork
configures environment variables to enable them).

tests: Add logic to benchmark IG

This commit adds logic to run benchmarking tests for IG. The testing
methodology is to run a steady workload that generates N events per
second, then to measure the CPU and memory usage on the system when
running with and without IG.

The benchmarks are configured by using a yaml file like this:

```
ntimes: 5
igPath: ig
igRuntime: "docker"
gadgetRunDuration: 20
warmUpDuration: 5
tests:
  - name: trace_dns
    gadgetName: trace_dns:v0.43.0
    # trace only the client container
    gadgetParams: ["--containername=test-trace_dns-client"]
    server:
      image: ghcr.io/mauriciovasquezbernal/bench
      cmd: /bench --events=dns-server
    generator:
      image: ghcr.io/mauriciovasquezbernal/bench
      cmd: /bench --events=dns:server={{.ServerIP}}:5353 --events-per-second={{.EventsPerSecond}}
    # at 8192 IG starts to drop packets
    eventsPerSecond: [ 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096 ]
...
```

It runs the tests for each gadget (using all the existing testing
infrastructure), and saves a csv file with the following data:
- CPU and memory usage of the whole host
- CPU and memory usage of the IG process

Tests are run multiple times according to ntimes, so we can provide
statistical data like the confidence interval.

ebpf operator: set map spec variables in gadget context

The ebpf operator uses gadgetCtx.SetVar() in the Start() method to
export ebpf maps to other operators. This cannot be done in PreStart()
because the maps can be changed by other operators. For example, the
socket enricher operator replaces the sockets ebpf map.

But the ustack operator needs to know at PreStart time if the gadget has
a user stack ebpf map. With this patch, the ebpf operator exports the
map specs under a different prefix at Instantiate time. Then, the ustack
operator can check a map presence at PreStart time.

Signed-off-by: Alban Crequy <alban.crequy@gmail.com>

ustack: use operator lifecycle correctly

According to the operator lifecycle documentation:
- InstantiateDataOperator: creates datasources. Called both in
  GetGadgetInfo and RunGadget
- PreStart: the operator subscribes to datasources
- Start: the operator starts emitting data (nothing to do in the case of
  the ustack operator)

This patch moves datasource subscription from Start to PreStart. This
ensure that ustack enrichment happens from the very first events.

This patch also instantiates the symbolizer in PreStart instead of
InstantiateDataOperator. The symbolizer is not needed for GetGadgetInfo.
The symbtab symbolizer is also not used client-side.

Signed-off-by: Alban Crequy <alban.crequy@gmail.com>

The FNV-1a hash functions are explained on Wikipedia:

The original implementation in the public domain:

Signed-off-by: Alban Crequy <alban.crequy@gmail.com>

ustack: cache the runtime base addresses

Due to Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), most processes have a
random base address chosen at execve-time.

Before this patch, IG parsed /proc/pid/maps to find the runtime base
address at each stack trace resolution. This patch adds a cache to
minimize the overhead.

The cache is not indexed by pid because:
- The base address changes with execve but the pid does not change at
  that time
- Several pids can share the same memory space with CLONE_VM (e.g.
  threads)

Instead, I use the mm_struct address to distinguish the programs sharing
the same base address. There are however a possibility where the
mm_struct address is reused: if the mm_struct is freed and re-allocated
to the same address. To avoid this scenario, I add mm->start_code and
mm->start_stack in the hash. A new program reusing the same mm_struct
address will have a different random start_code and start_stack.

To reduce the size of events sent to the ebpf ring buffer, we send a u32
hash:

```c
	// Identify the base address.
	// Changes whenever the base address changes at execve.
	// Not shared between processes because of Address Space Layout Randomization.
	// FNV-1a hash of tuple (mm_addr, start_code, start_stack)
	__u32 base_addr_hash;
```

I chose the hash algorithm FNV-1a because it is fast and easy to
implement in ebpf. It is not cryptographically secure but the 3
components of the tuple (mm_addr, start_code, start_stack) are chosen by
the kernel.

Note that the base address cannot reliably be found from ebpf. Even
though mm_struct has fields like start_code and start_data, that does
not directly give the base address. The information could be found in
kernel space by iterating over the VMAs but this cannot be done in ebpf
because that would be an unbounded loop.

Example:
```
$ sudo cat /proc/1853244/maps
55f86c7ec000-55f86c7ed000 r--p 00000000 08:16 23894993                   /usr/local/bin/python3.13
55f86c7ed000-55f86c7ee000 r-xp 00001000 08:16 23894993                   /usr/local/bin/python3.13
55f86c7ee000-55f86c7ef000 r--p 00002000 08:16 23894993                   /usr/local/bin/python3.13
55f86c7ef000-55f86c7f0000 r--p 00002000 08:16 23894993                   /usr/local/bin/python3.13
55f86c7f0000-55f86c7f1000 rw-p 00003000 08:16 23894993                   /usr/local/bin/python3.13
...
55f86d141000-55f86d704000 rw-p 00000000 00:00 0                          [heap]
...
7ffd65563000-7ffd65584000 rw-p 00000000 00:00 0                          [stack]
```

mm_struct fields (found by modifying the snapshot_process gadget):

| Field Name       | Address (Hexadecimal) |
| :---             | :---                  |
| **start_code**   | 55f86c7ed000          |
| **end_code**     | 55f86c7ed155          |
| **start_data**   | 55f86c7efdb0          |
| **end_data**     | 55f86c7f0018          |
| **start_brk**    | 55f86d141000          |
| **start_stack**  | 7ffd65583590          |

The base address is 55f86c7ec000 and the start_code is 55f86c7ed000
(8KiB below). While it is often 8KiB in practice, we cannot rely on
that. It is 8KiB here because the first LOAD segment has a size of 8KiB
(after rounding up on the page size). It typically contains metadata
like the ELF header, the program headers and the interpreter path
("/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2"). Other programs might be compiled
differently.

```
$ sudo readelf -lW /usr/local/bin/python3.13
Program Headers:
  Type           Offset   VirtAddr           PhysAddr           FileSiz  MemSiz   Flg Align
  PHDR           0x000040 0x0000000000000040 0x0000000000000040 0x000310 0x000310 R   0x8
  INTERP         0x000394 0x0000000000000394 0x0000000000000394 0x00001c 0x00001c R   0x1
      [Requesting program interpreter: /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2]
  LOAD           0x000000 0x0000000000000000 0x0000000000000000 0x000760 0x000760 R   0x1000
  LOAD           0x001000 0x0000000000001000 0x0000000000001000 0x000155 0x000155 R E 0x1000
  LOAD           0x002000 0x0000000000002000 0x0000000000002000 0x0000f0 0x0000f0 R   0x1000
  LOAD           0x002db0 0x0000000000003db0 0x0000000000003db0 0x000268 0x000270 RW  0x1000
...
```

docker run --rm -ti --name gcclatest ghcr.io/inspektor-gadget/ci/gcc:latest nsenter --setuid 1000 --setgid 1111 /usr/bin/sh -c '/bin/echo OK'

kallsyms/cache: preload kallsyms that cilium/ebpf will need

Introduce a new package pkg/kallsyms/cache used by:
- kfilefield
- container-hook
- kfilefields

The cost of loading many symbols at once is lower than loading few
symbols multiple times for multiple ebpf collections. This is because
most of the cpu time is used for reading /proc/kallsyms in the kernel
function module_get_kallsym. So it is better to read /proc/kallsyms only
one time.
https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/v6.15/kernel/module/kallsyms.c#L376

The cache package provides two separate functions:
- RegisterSymbolsFromSpec: to be called from init()
- PopulateKallsymsCache: to be called just before loading your ebpf
  collection

In this way, different users of the cache don't have to collaborate to
collect the symbols they use.

socketenricher: Use CO-RE to make it resilient against changes

The socketenricher operator is used  to enrich events with process
information from a socket. This is implemented as an ebpf map that
stores a list of tuples (IPs+ports) and the information of the process
that created the socket. This map is an API contract between the gadgets
and Inspektor Gadget, any change to the layout of the data on it will
require the gadgets to be recompiled. Of course, this is a very big
limitation.

This commit uses the existing CO-RE technology to make it possible to
update the layout of this map without breaking the gadgets. This is done
by generating a BTF data that represents the structure stored on this map,
then this data is fed to the ebpf-go library when loading the program,
ensuring it relocates the access to that structure.

This in practice allows to:
- Introduce new information to the socket enricher
- Change the type or position of existing fields on it
- Dynamically disable or reduce the maximum size of some expensive fields (like paths).
  - Reduce the size of the map
  - Avoid spending CPU cycles on disabled fields

gadgetCtx: add IsClient

Some operators are used both server-side and client-side. Soon, the
ustack operator will also be able to operator client-side and
server-side.

The IsClient method allows to detect which side they are running and
behave differently. This is similar to IsRemoteCall to detect if we are
on a server.

Command           | IsClient | IsRemoteCall |
------------------|----------|--------------|
ig run            | false    | false        |
ig image inspect  | false    | false        |
ig daemon         | false    | true         |
gadgetctl run     | true     | false (*)    |

*: Note that gadgetctl can display logs from the server, so gadgetctl
will print both lines:
    client=true, remote_call=false
    client=false, remote_call=true
Depending if the log was generated from the server or the client.

trace_exec: fix test for nsenter from util-linux 2.41

nsenter from util-linux 2.38.1 used to be able to set some options like
setuid and setgid without changing namespaces:

docker run --rm -ti --name gcctest ghcr.io/inspektor-gadget/ci/gcc:test nsenter --setuid 1000 --setgid 1111 /usr/bin/sh -c '/bin/echo OK'
OK

docker run --rm -ti --name gcclatest ghcr.io/inspektor-gadget/ci/gcc:latest nsenter --setuid 1000 --setgid 1111 /usr/bin/sh -c '/bin/echo OK'
nsenter: no namespace specified

This patch changes the command line to use setpriv instead of nsenter.

security: add VEX documents

VEX documents to provide a clear, machine-readable
assessment of our software's relationship to known vulnerabilities (CVEs). VEX
helps users and security tools to:
- Suppress false positives for vulnerabilities that do not affect our project.
- Understand why a specific vulnerability is or is not exploitable in our code.

This patch adds VEX documents in the .vex directory, making it easily
discoverable by tools such as VEX Hub (https://github.com/aquasecurity/vexhub).

Once merged, I plan to add the VEX documents as assets attached to the
GitHub releases as suggested by the document id ("@id":
https://github.com/inspektor-gadget/inspektor-gadget/releases/download/v0.41.0/v0.41.0.vex.json).

In these initial VEX documents, I only go back to v0.41.0 because it's
the last release with builtin gadgets, and I have not heard of user
interest to go further back.

To generate the VEX documents, I used the vexctl command as explained in
docs/SECURITY.md.

tests: Add logic to benchmark IG

This commit adds logic to run benchmarking tests for IG. The testing
methodology is to run a steady workload that generates N events per
second, then to measure the CPU and memory usage on the system when
running with and without IG.

The benchmarks are configured by using a yaml file like this:

```
ntimes: 5
igPath: ig
igRuntime: "docker"
gadgetRunDuration: 20
warmUpDuration: 5
tests:
  - name: trace_dns
    gadgetName: trace_dns:v0.43.0
    # trace only the client container
    gadgetParams: ["--containername=test-trace_dns-client"]
    server:
      image: ghcr.io/mauriciovasquezbernal/bench
      cmd: /bench --events=dns-server
    generator:
      image: ghcr.io/mauriciovasquezbernal/bench
      cmd: /bench --events=dns:server={{.ServerIP}}:5353 --events-per-second={{.EventsPerSecond}}
    # at 8192 IG starts to drop packets
    eventsPerSecond: [ 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096 ]
...
```

It runs the tests for each gadget (using all the existing testing
infrastructure), and saves a csv file with the following data:
- CPU and memory usage of the whole host
- CPU and memory usage of the IG process

Tests are run multiple times according to ntimes, so we can provide
statistical data like the confidence interval.

ustack: use operator lifecycle correctly

- InstantiateDataOperator: creates datasources. Called both in

- PreStart: the operator subscribes to datasources

ustack: cache the runtime base addresses

Due to Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), most processes have a
random base address chosen at execve-time.

Before this patch, IG parsed /proc/pid/maps to find the runtime base
address at each stack trace resolution. This patch adds a cache to
minimize the overhead.

The cache is not indexed by pid because:
- The base address changes with execve but the pid does not change at
  that time
- Several pids can share the same memory space with CLONE_VM (e.g.
  threads)

Instead, I use the mm_struct address to distinguish the programs sharing
the same base address. There are however a possibility where the
mm_struct address is reused: if the mm_struct is freed and re-allocated
to the same address. To avoid this scenario, I add mm->start_code and
mm->start_stack in the hash. A new program reusing the same mm_struct
address will have a different random start_code and start_stack.

To reduce the size of events sent to the ebpf ring buffer, we send a u32
hash:

```c
	// Identify the base address.
	// Changes whenever the base address changes at execve.
	// Not shared between processes because of Address Space Layout Randomization.
	// FNV-1a hash of tuple (mm_addr, start_code, start_stack)
	__u32 base_addr_hash;
```

I chose the hash algorithm FNV-1a because it is fast and easy to
implement in ebpf. It is not cryptographically secure but the 3
components of the tuple (mm_addr, start_code, start_stack) are chosen by
the kernel.

Note that the base address cannot reliably be found from ebpf. Even
though mm_struct has fields like start_code and start_data, that does
not directly give the base address. The information could be found in
kernel space by iterating over the VMAs but this cannot be done in ebpf
because that would be an unbounded loop.

Example:
```
$ sudo cat /proc/1853244/maps
55f86c7ec000-55f86c7ed000 r--p 00000000 08:16 23894993                   /usr/local/bin/python3.13
55f86c7ed000-55f86c7ee000 r-xp 00001000 08:16 23894993                   /usr/local/bin/python3.13
55f86c7ee000-55f86c7ef000 r--p 00002000 08:16 23894993                   /usr/local/bin/python3.13
55f86c7ef000-55f86c7f0000 r--p 00002000 08:16 23894993                   /usr/local/bin/python3.13
55f86c7f0000-55f86c7f1000 rw-p 00003000 08:16 23894993                   /usr/local/bin/python3.13
...
55f86d141000-55f86d704000 rw-p 00000000 00:00 0                          [heap]
...
7ffd65563000-7ffd65584000 rw-p 00000000 00:00 0                          [stack]
```

Signed-off-by: Mauricio Vásquez <mauriciov@microsoft.com>

enrich: Do not try to enrich multiple times

Inspektor Gadget is able to enrich events by using the mount namespace
or the network namespace. The previous implementation had an issue as
it first tried to enrich the mount namespace, and then with the network
namespace. This caused the specific information provided by the mount ns
(like the container in a pod) to be lost as it was overwritten by the
net ns enrichment. (the network namespace is shared by all containers
on the same pod so it's not possible to distinguish among them when
enrichment with this field). This commit fixes that logic by introducing
some logic that avoid to perform a second enrichment if the first one
succeded.

Fixes: b1875da7aed0 ("pkg/types: add wrapper for events to implement interfaces for compatibility")
Reported-by: Matthias Bertschy <matthias.bertschy@gmail.com>

gadgets: fix off-by-one error in log2 histogram slot calculation

The histogram gadgets were assigning samples to the wrong buckets because the kernel-side code used a 0-based log2 index (floor(log2(v))) while the userspace histogram printer expects 1-based log2 buckets, matching bcc’s bpf_log2l() convention:
  0: 0 -> 1
  1: 1 -> 2
  2: 2 -> 4
  ...

Because of this mismatch, every non-zero value appeared in the previous bucket. For example, a 300 ms latency (~300000 µs) was placed in the "131072 -> 262144" slot instead of "262144 -> 524288".

This commit introduces get_slot_idx(), which returns 0 for v == 0 and floor(log2(v)) + 1 for v > 0, ensuring that kernel-side indices match the expected histogram ranges. As a result, latency profiles now report values in the correct slots.

cmd: Remove possibility to customize CFLAGS from build.yaml.

Before this commit, it was possible to customize CFLAGS from a gadget build.yaml
file by using the "cflags" key.
This feature could be abuse to inject shell command in Makefile.build.
For example, having a gadget with the following build.yaml:
ebpfsource: "program.bpf.c"
metadata: "gadget.yaml"
cflags: "; touch poc.txt;"
Would then lead the clang line to be expanded like in the Makefile.build:
$(CLANG) $(BASECFLAGS) $(subst @ARCH@,$*,$(CFLAGS)) -D __TARGET_ARCH_$(subst amd64,x86,$*) \
		-c $< -I /usr/include/gadget/$*/ -o $@
clang -target bpf -Wall -g -O2 -I/usr/include/$(shell uname -m)-linux-gnu; touch poc.txt; -D __TARGET_ARCH_$(subst amd64,x86,$*) \
		-c $< -I /usr/include/gadget/$*/ -o $@
So, the Makefile.build would then execute the nasty command given in the
build.yaml.

As a consequence, this commit removes totally the possibility to customize
CFLAGS from build.yaml. Indeed, since its introduction, this feature was almost
never used.

containers: Avoid blocking creation of new containers

Inspektor Gadget keeps a reference of the mount namespace few seconds
after a container has been terminated in order to avoid its inode to be
reused by newer containers which causes a race condition when enriching
events [0].

This reference is closed few seconds after the container is terminated,
however, if the container had a nfs mount when terminated, this call
gets blocked (up to 6mins in our testing), which causes the whole
container creation logic to get stuck, i.e. not new containers can be
created on the system.

In order to avoid this issue, this commits moves this logic into an
independent goroutine.

[0]: 4dedafc8565d ("Fix race condition on enrichers")

cmd: Remove possibility to customize CFLAGS from build.yaml.

Before this commit, it was possible to customize CFLAGS from a gadget build.yaml
file by using the "cflags" key.
This feature could be abuse to inject shell command in Makefile.build.
For example, having a gadget with the following build.yaml:
ebpfsource: "program.bpf.c"
metadata: "gadget.yaml"
cflags: "; touch poc.txt;"
Would then lead the clang line to be expanded like in the Makefile.build:
$(CLANG) $(BASECFLAGS) $(subst @ARCH@,$*,$(CFLAGS)) -D __TARGET_ARCH_$(subst amd64,x86,$*) \
		-c $< -I /usr/include/gadget/$*/ -o $@
clang -target bpf -Wall -g -O2 -I/usr/include/$(shell uname -m)-linux-gnu; touch poc.txt; -D __TARGET_ARCH_$(subst amd64,x86,$*) \
		-c $< -I /usr/include/gadget/$*/ -o $@
So, the Makefile.build would then execute the nasty command given in the
build.yaml.

As a consequence, this commit removes totally the possibility to customize
CFLAGS from build.yaml. Indeed, since its introduction, this feature was almost
never used.

Fixes: da4727389ce1 ("cmd: Update image build command to actually build the eBPF bytecode")

pkg: columns: Escape strings before printing them.

The columns output did not run any sanitization of the output before printing it
which could lead to terminal interpreting escape sequence.
Consider the following C code:
open("/etc/shadow", O_RDONLY);
// ...
open("/etc\x1b[1A/bashrc\x1b[1B\x1b[13C", O_CREAT | O_WRONLY | O_TRUNC, 0644);
The first open() opens /etc/shadow, while the second open() creates a file which
names contains shell escape sequence.
With the current behavior, the trace_open gadget output is modified by the shell
escape sequence to hide the malicious read to /etc/shadow:
RUNTIME.CONTAINERN… COMM               PID        TID TID         FD FNAME                    FPATH                    ERROR   MODE
...
poc-escape-inject   escape_inj…      25641      25641 25591        3 /etc/bashrc                                               ----------
poc-escape-inject   escape_inj…      25641      25641 25591        0 /etc                                              ENOENT  -rw-r--r--

By using strconv.Quote() on the strings which are about to be outputted, we
prevent the escape sequence to be interpreted and the output is now correct:
RUNTIME.CONTAINERN… COMM               PID        TID TID         FD FNAME                    FPATH                    ERROR   MODE
...
poc-escape-inject   escape_inj…     116656     116656 116605       3 /etc/shadow                                               ----------
poc-escape-inject   escape_inj…     116656     116656 116605       0 /etc\x1b[1A/bashrc\x1b[…                          ENOENT  -rw-r--r--

Fixes: GHSA-34r5-6j7w-235f ("Unsanitized ANSI Escape Sequences In `columns` Output Mode")
Reported-by: Nicolò Daprelà <nicolo.daprela@shielder.it>
Reported-by: Pietro Tirenna <pietro.tirenna@shielder.it>
Signed-off-by: Francis Laniel <flaniel@linux.microsoft.com>

pkg/signature: Fix exporting/pulling OCI 1.1 signature.

Before, we were only relying on the sha256-digest tag, but this is only used if
the registry does not support the referrers API [1].
The code targeting OCI 1.1 was enhanced to find the signature contained in OCI
1.1 by first using the referrers API and then the sha256-digest tag.

Fixes: 939c61807d88 ("pkg: signature: cosign: Add OCI 1.1 way to retrieve cosign signature.")
Signed-off-by: Francis Laniel <flaniel@linux.microsoft.com>
[1]: https://github.com/opencontainers/distribution-spec/blob/v1.1.1/spec.md#referrers-tag-schema

go.mod: Use fork of notation-go.

Depending on Notation version used to sign the OCI image, the type of
config.mediaType can be different:
1. "application/vnd.cncf.notary.signature", in older Notation.
2. "application/vnd.oci.empty.v1+json", in newer Notation.

The current version of notation-go does not support the second, but it exists a
commit upstream which adds support for the second [1].
Unfortunately, there is no release with this commit and using the main branch
triggers some false positive for CVEs.
So, this commit use our fork of notation-go. This way, we can support the second
case mentioned above.

Signed-off-by: Francis Laniel <flaniel@linux.microsoft.com>
[1]: https://github.com/notaryproject/notation-go/commit/de3655adc0cb

pkg: columns: Escape strings before printing them.

The columns output did not run any sanitization of the output before printing it
which could lead to terminal interpreting escape sequence.
Consider the following C code:
open("/etc/shadow", O_RDONLY);
// ...
open("/etc\x1b[1A/bashrc\x1b[1B\x1b[13C", O_CREAT | O_WRONLY | O_TRUNC, 0644);
The first open() opens /etc/shadow, while the second open() creates a file which
names contains shell escape sequence.
With the current behavior, the trace_open gadget output is modified by the shell
escape sequence to hide the malicious read to /etc/shadow:
RUNTIME.CONTAINERN… COMM               PID        TID TID         FD FNAME                    FPATH                    ERROR   MODE
...
poc-escape-inject   escape_inj…      25641      25641 25591        3 /etc/bashrc                                               ----------
poc-escape-inject   escape_inj…      25641      25641 25591        0 /etc                                              ENOENT  -rw-r--r--

By using strconv.Quote() on the strings which are about to be outputted, we
prevent the escape sequence to be interpreted and the output is now correct:
RUNTIME.CONTAINERN… COMM               PID        TID TID         FD FNAME                    FPATH                    ERROR   MODE
...
poc-escape-inject   escape_inj…     116656     116656 116605       3 /etc/shadow                                               ----------
poc-escape-inject   escape_inj…     116656     116656 116605       0 /etc\x1b[1A/bashrc\x1b[…                          ENOENT  -rw-r--r--

Fixes: GHSA-34r5-6j7w-235f ("Unsanitized ANSI Escape Sequences In `columns` Output Mode")

include: Add maps dedicated to count ring buffer lost samples.

Contrary to perf buffer, ring buffer does not offer a mechanism to count lost
samples.
So, when bpf_ringbuf_reserve() returns NULL, i.e. when the ring buffer is full,
there is no way for user space to know about this.

This commit modifies the GADGET_TRACER_MAP macro in order to create a per cpu
array corresponding to the ring buffer. This per cpu array would be used to
count the number of lost samples when bpf_ringbuf_reserve() returns NULL.
Accordingly, the gadget_reserve_buf() was converted to a macro to get the
corresponding per cpu array from the ring buffer name.
The value stored in the per cpu array is read and reset by user space to inform
about lost samples. To avoid decreasing the performance, this occurs
periodically in a go routine.

include: Add maps dedicated to count ring buffer lost samples.

Contrary to perf buffer, ring buffer does not offer a mechanism to count lost
samples.
So, when bpf_ringbuf_reserve() returns NULL, i.e. when the ring buffer is full,
there is no way for user space to know about this.

This commit modifies the GADGET_TRACER_MAP macro in order to create a per cpu
array corresponding to the ring buffer. This per cpu array would be used to
count the number of lost samples when bpf_ringbuf_reserve() returns NULL.
Accordingly, the gadget_reserve_buf() was converted to a macro to get the
corresponding per cpu array from the ring buffer name.
The value stored in the per cpu array is read and reset by user space to inform
about lost samples. To avoid decreasing the performance, this occurs
periodically in a go routine.

ci: Bump azure/aks-set-context from 4.0.3 to 5.0.0

Add top_cpu_throttle gadget to detect CFS bandwidth throttling

Add a new 'top_cpu_throttle' gadget that periodically reads cgroup v2
files (cpu.stat, cpu.max, cpu.pressure) and ranks containers by CFS
throttle severity. This helps identify pods suffering from CPU pressure
due to tight cgroup CPU limits rather than actual CPU overutilization.

The gadget is implemented as a pure userspace operator (no eBPF) following
the existing top_process operator pattern. It computes per-interval deltas
for throttle counters and reports:

- Throttle counts and ratios per cgroup
- CPU quota, period, and effective core limit
- Time spent throttled (human-readable via gadget_duration)
- PSI 'some' pressure averages (10s/60s) when available

Cgroups without an explicit CPU bandwidth limit are filtered out.
PSI 'full' metrics are omitted since CFS throttling is all-or-nothing
at the cgroup level, making 'full' always identical to 'some'.

fix(oci): preserve OCI 1.1 referrer artifacts during image import

ImportGadgetImages() only iterated over tagged entries via src.Tags(),
so untagged OCI 1.1 referrer manifests (e.g. notation signatures with
a subject field but no tag annotation) were silently dropped during
import. This broke air-gapped notation signature verification.

Replace oras.Copy with oras.ExtendedCopy which automatically traverses
the predecessor/referrer graph and copies associated artifacts alongside
the tagged image. No impact on cosign .sig tags or images without
referrers.

Add TestExtendedCopyPreservesReferrers to validate that ExtendedCopy
preserves untagged referrer manifests while plain Copy does not.

gadget-container/entrypoint: Fix symlink crash loop on container restart

prepareGadgetPullSecret() creates a symlink from /var/lib/ig/config.json
to the mounted pull secret. Since /var/lib/ig is backed by an emptyDir
volume, the symlink persists across container restarts. On restart,
os.Symlink fails with EEXIST, causing a fatal error that puts the
container into a permanent CrashLoopBackOff.

Use os.Lstat to check if the path already exists before creating the
symlink. If it is already a symlink, skip creation. If it exists but
is not a symlink, return an error to avoid overwriting important files.

profile_cuda: reduce BPF stack frame size for older kernels

Move struct gadget_user_stack and struct alloc_val from stack-local
variables to per-CPU array maps in gen_alloc_exit(). This reduces the
BPF stack frame by ~216 bytes (72B + 144B), bringing it well under the
256-byte limit.

The 256-byte limit is enforced by the BPF verifier on kernels < 6.13
when a function contains both BPF-to-BPF subprogram calls and tail
calls. Upcoming work on OTel eBPF Profiler symbolization (PR #4925) will
add a noinline function with bpf_tail_call() inside
gadget_get_user_stack(), which triggers this check. With the original
~248-byte stack frame, the verifier would reject the program on kernels
5.4 through 6.6.

Linux 6.13 introduces private stack support (PRIV_STACK_ADAPTIVE) for
kprobe programs, which allocates each subprogram's stack independently
and avoids the cumulative depth check entirely.

Signed-off-by: Alban Crequy <alban.crequy@gmail.com>
Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>

profile_cpu: reduce BPF stack frame size for older kernels

Move struct key_t from a stack-local variable to a per-CPU array map.
This reduces the BPF stack frame by ~148 bytes, avoiding the 256-byte
verifier limit when tail calls are combined with BPF-to-BPF subprogram
calls on kernels < 6.13. See the previous commit for details.

The per-CPU array element is zeroed before use via bpf_map_update_elem
with a static const zero-initialized key, since key_t is used as a hash
map key and must not contain stale data from previous invocations.

oci: release oras target after operators are instantiated

The GadgetContext holds the oras ReadOnlyTarget (and its internal blob
cache) while image operators are calling InstantiateImageOperator to read
OCI layers. Once all data operators have been instantiated the store is
no longer accessed, yet the reference was kept for the gadget's entire
lifetime (~28 MiB per gadget process).

Clear c.orasTarget at the end of instantiateOperators() and document the
lifetime in WithOrasReadonlyTarget() so callers know OrasTarget() is
only guaranteed to return a usable value up to that point. Releasing it
inside GadgetContext (the owner) keeps the lifecycle in one place rather
than delegating it to a specific operator.

The raw ELF/BPF object bytes read by InstantiateImageOperator are stored
in ebpfInstance.program and used only by loadSpec() and addExtraInfo().
Once both have completed the bytes are never accessed again, yet they
are retained for the lifetime of the gadget (~28 MiB per gadget process).

can reclaim that memory before the gadget enters its run loop.

ebpf: release CollectionSpec after programs are attached

The CollectionSpec holds ~30 MiB of BTF type/line info and BPF program
bytecode that is needed only during loading and CO-RE relocation.
After all programs are attached and iterators are running the spec is
no longer referenced at runtime, so setting it to nil allows the GC to
reclaim that memory.

Measured saving: ~30 MiB of Go heap inuse per gadget process that
loads eBPF programs via inspektor-gadget.

otel: plumb resolved stacks into symbols field

Add a replacement stack mechanism to the Resolve() interface: when the
OTel resolver has more frames than the kernel stack (e.g. interpreted
language frames), it returns a replacement []StackItemResponse. The
symbolizer chain detects this and uses it directly, skipping remaining
resolvers since native addresses don't correspond to interpreted frames.

Based on work by Mauricio Vásquez <mauriciov@microsoft.com>.

Signed-off-by: Alban Crequy <alban.crequy@gmail.com>

docs: add OTel eBPF Profiler architecture document

Signed-off-by: Alban Crequy <alban.crequy@gmail.com>

otel: replace time.Sleep with per-correlation-id channel synchronization

Replace the time.Sleep(1s) hack with a proper synchronization mechanism
using per-correlation-id channels. When Resolve() does not find a
correlation ID in the map, it registers a waiter channel and blocks until
the traceReporter callback signals arrival by closing the channel, or
until an 800ms timeout expires.

Multiple consumers (from different datasources in the same gadget) can
safely wait on the same correlation ID by sharing the same channel.

Add a boot_timestamp field (from bpf_ktime_get_boot_ns) to struct
gadget_user_stack to support adaptive timeouts: the remaining wait time
is reduced by the time already elapsed since the BPF event was produced.
This prevents unbounded lag when OTel fails to unwind certain stacks,
since backlogged events skip the wait instead of each blocking for the
full timeout. Older gadgets without this field fall back to the fixed
800ms timeout.

Also fix a pre-existing data race: correlationMap was accessed without
synchronization from the OTel map monitor goroutine (producer) and the
ustack operator goroutine(s) (consumers). A sync.Mutex now protects both
correlationMap and the waiters map.

Signed-off-by: Alban Crequy <alban.crequy@gmail.com>

otel: fix generic_params map key type to match OTel definition

Change the key type of otel_generic_params from u32 to int to match the
OTel eBPF Profiler's generic_params map definition in
support/ebpf/interpreter_dispatcher.ebpf.c. The cilium/ebpf
Compatible() check compares BTF types, and u32 vs int are considered
incompatible even though both are 4 bytes. This caused the map
replacement to silently fail, resulting in the gadget and OTel using
separate generic_params maps with different correlation IDs.

otel: implement correlationMap cleanup via BPF LRU map pruning

Add two-cycle pruning of stale correlationMap entries by
cross-referencing the BPF LRU stack cache map. On each prune
cycle, correlation IDs absent from the BPF map are marked as
candidates; they are only deleted if still absent on the next
cycle. This grace period ensures in-flight events have time to
be consumed by lookupOrWait before their frames are removed.

If BPF map iteration is aborted (e.g. LRU evicts the iterator's
cursor key due to concurrent BPF activity), the entire prune
cycle is skipped to avoid premature deletion from partial data.

Update the OTel dependency to pick up the LRU hash map change
(BPF_MAP_TYPE_LRU_HASH with max_entries=256) and the new
GetStackCacheMap() accessor.

gadgets/trace_capabilities: reduce current_syscall map size from 1M to 10K

The current_syscall map uses BPF_MAP_TYPE_HASH which pre-allocates all
entries at load time. With max_entries=1048576, key=u32 and value=u64,
the kernel allocates roughly 44 MiB per map instance (36 bytes/entry +
8 MiB bucket array).

The comment copied from trace_exec ("many threads sleeping in futex/poll")
does not apply here: capability checks via cap_capable are momentary kernel
calls, not long-sleeping syscalls. The map is also used to track execve
context across thread group leader handoff, but even that scenario cannot
produce anywhere near 1M simultaneous entries.

10240 matches the other maps in this file and is generous for the workload.

Savings: ~43 MiB of kernel memory per gadget instance.

Signed-off-by: Matthias Bertschy <matthias.bertschy@gmail.com>

ustack,ebpf,symbolizer: remove [N] prefix from stack symbols and show binary+offset

Remove the [N] index prefix from stack trace symbols to improve
flamegraph rendering. Previously, each symbol was prefixed with its
position (e.g., [0]funcA; [1]funcB;) which prevented flamegraph tools
from collapsing identical function names across different stack traces.

For unresolved symbols in the otel-ebpf-profiler path, show the
mapping file name and address offset (e.g., libcudart.so.12+0x1234)
instead of leaving the entry empty.

For unresolved symbols without otel, fall back to showing the raw
address (0x...) to ensure no empty entries appear in the output.

Fixes: https://github.com/inspektor-gadget/inspektor-gadget/issues/5505

gadgets/top_cuda_memory: Fix implicit free on thread exit

sched_process_free runs for every released task_struct, and
bpf_get_current_pid_tgid() does not identify the task being freed from
that tracepoint. This could make top_cuda_memory account remaining CUDA
memory as implicitly freed while the CUDA process was still running.

Use the freed task pid from the sched_process_free tracepoint payload
instead. Calling handle_ctx_destroy() for every freed task is safe because
the outstanding maps are keyed by thread-group id: non-leader tids do not
match any outstanding entry and become no-ops, while the leader pid matches
when the process is finally released.

Also keep comm and mntns_id in the outstanding allocation state so
implicit-free rows can be reported with process metadata captured from a
reliable CUDA allocation context, instead of reading current task metadata
from sched_process_free.

Signed-off-by: Burak Ok <burakok@microsoft.com>

pkg/utils/safeelf: Add panic-safe wrapper for debug/elf

The Go standard library's debug/elf package is explicitly not hardened
against adversarial inputs: "parsing malformed files may consume
significant resources, or cause panics" (Go documentation). Since
Inspektor Gadget parses ELF files from untrusted containers in a
privileged process, a crafted binary could crash the daemon.

Add a safeelf package (inspired by cilium/ebpf's internal/elf.go) that
wraps debug/elf operations with defer/recover to convert panics into
errors. The wrapper covers NewFile, Symbols, and DynamicSymbols.

Update all callsites that parse untrusted ELF files to use safeelf:
- pkg/uprobetracer/usdt.go (USDT note parsing)
- pkg/symbolizer/table.go (container binary symbol lookup)
- pkg/operators/ebpf/extrainfo.go (gadget ELF metadata)

Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>
Signed-off-by: Alban Crequy <albancrequy@microsoft.com>

uprobetracer: Harden USDT note parsing against malicious ELF files

A crafted ELF file inside a container could crash the privileged
Inspektor Gadget process by triggering a panic or excessive memory
allocation in getUsdtInfo():

- A stapsdt note with DescSize smaller than 3*wordSize causes an
  out-of-bounds slice access on desc[:wordSize] (panic).
- A note with a very large NameSize or DescSize causes excessive
  memory allocation (DoS).

Fix by:
- Adding a bounds check on desc length before accessing address fields.
- Capping note name/desc sizes to 1 MiB to prevent memory exhaustion.

Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>
Signed-off-by: Alban Crequy <albancrequy@microsoft.com>

symbolizer: Check MaxSymbolCount inside loop to bound memory usage

Previously, MaxSymbolCount was checked after iterating over all ELF
symbols and appending them to the slice. A binary with millions of
symbols could cause excessive peak memory allocation before the check
triggers and rejects the file.

Move the check inside the loop so that parsing bails out immediately
once the limit is exceeded, bounding peak memory to roughly
MaxSymbolCount * sizeof(Symbol).

Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>
Signed-off-by: Alban Crequy <albancrequy@microsoft.com>

uprobetracer: Fix CPU denial of service in ld.so.cache parser

A crafted /etc/ld.so.cache in an unprivileged container can cause ~57
seconds of CPU burn when uprobe-based gadgets are active. During this
time, the fanotify container-hook holds the container startup pause,
blocking Docker from starting any other container on the host.

Root causes and fixes:

1. readStringFromBytes used O(n²) string concatenation (one byte at a
   time). Replace with O(n) bytes.IndexByte + single slice conversion.

2. EntryCount read from the untrusted file drove the parsing loop
   without a cap. Add a maximum based on actual file size before
   iterating, for both format1 and format2.

3. cache1Len computation used uint32 arithmetic, overflowing with
   crafted EntryCount values. Use uint64 arithmetic.

4. Missing bounds checks before slice accesses on short files. Add
   length checks for defense in depth.

5. encoding/binary.Read used reflection to decode each entry struct
   (~700K calls). Replace with direct unsafe.Pointer reinterpretation,
   constrained by a plainDataStruct type union that only permits
   fixed-size numeric structs (compile-time safety).

6. All ~700K entries were collected into a []ldEntry slice then
   filtered. Instead, filter inline during parsing using
   matchStringInBytes (prefix check without allocation), only
   allocating strings for matching entries.

7. Cap matching results to 64 entries per library lookup (a real
   ld.so.cache has only 1-3 entries per library). This bounds memory
   when a crafted file has all entries matching the same prefix. (Review
   from Mauricio Vásquez)

Signed-off-by: Alban Crequy <albancrequy@microsoft.com>

container-hook: avoid fanotify self-deadlock by caching config.json

The fanotify watcher goroutine watchPidFileIterate() needs to read
the OCI bundle config.json after detecting a new pidfile. Until now,
that read was done with os.Open()+io.ReadAll() *after* the bundle
directory had been marked with FAN_ACCESS_PERM|FAN_EVENT_ON_CHILD on
the same fanotify fd that this goroutine itself drains.

On Linux >= 5.9 we mitigate that with a FAN_MARK_IGNORED_MASK on
config.json so the listener's own read does not generate a permission
event. Kernel commit 497b0c5a7c06 (5.9) is what makes that ignore
mask work when the parent directory is the watched object; on older
kernels the ignore mask is silently bypassed and the read *does*
generate an event on our own fd. Since watchPidFileIterate is the
single consumer of that fd, the read() then blocks indefinitely
waiting for a FAN_ALLOW that only itself can emit -- a hard
self-deadlock.

Verified the kernel behavior with two small reproducers (a sibling
ignore-mask check and a same-thread hold-event-then-read check)
under vimto on cilium ci-kernels 5.4.296 (broken, deadlocks) and
5.15.202 / 6.16 (fixed).

Commit bc0b46328 ("container-hook: introduce PreCreateContainer
events") added a second config.json read inside
callPreCreateContainerCallback(), this time on watchRuntimeBinary's
critical section while runc's execve is still blocked on
FAN_OPEN_EXEC_PERM. Even when the kernel doesn't deadlock outright,
that read serialises every container start behind whatever
watchPendingContainers is currently draining.

Read config.json into memory once in monitorRuntimeInstance, BEFORE
adding any fanotify mark on the bundle directory, and cache the
bytes in pendingContainer.configJSON. Both downstream consumers
(watchPidFileIterate and callPreCreateContainerCallback) use the
cached bytes. The ignore mask on config.json is kept to silence
runc / runc-init reads on >= 5.9 kernels (no-op on older ones).

Fixes: bc0b46328 ("container-hook: introduce PreCreateContainer events")

Signed-off-by: Alban Crequy <albancrequy@microsoft.com>

operators/generate_networkpolicy: add Cilium NetworkPolicy format

Add a --policy-format flag to advise_networkpolicy with two values:
- "k8s" (default): existing networking.k8s.io/v1 NetworkPolicy output
- "cilium": new cilium.io/v2 CiliumNetworkPolicy output

The Cilium format differs from the K8s one in two ways:
- Cross-namespace peers are expressed via io.kubernetes.pod.namespace
  in matchLabels (endpointSelector/fromEndpoints/toEndpoints) instead
  of a separate namespaceSelector field.
- Ports for the same peer endpoint are grouped into a single rule
  (toPorts list), producing shorter and easier-to-read policies.

ci: remove SBOMs from image index, sign them separately

Remove SBOM digests from the `imagetools create` calls in
publish-gadget-images-manifest and publish-ig-images-manifest.
The image index now contains only platform images.

The `oras attach` step creates SBOM artifacts with platform
linux and an empty architecture string. Including these in the
index produced entries with platform linux/"" that break
registries mirroring the index verbatim (e.g. AWS ECR
pull-through cache), causing arm64 pull failures.

SBOMs remain attached to per-platform images via `oras attach`
and are discoverable through the OCI referrers API. SBOM signing
is done in the matrix build jobs right after oras attach, leveraging
the existing matrix.platform parameter.

Signed-off-by: natejsimonsen <natejsimonsen@gmail.com>

oci: Ensure oci-store dir exists before locking

Currently in newLocalOciStore() we only ensure that '/var/lib/ig'
exists (triming the 'oci-store' using file filepath.Dir) this cause
an issue with flock based lock since it needs the '/var/lib/ig/oci-store'
to be present before being able to create the lock file. We only hit
the issue on a fresh start of IG pods because when of one the racy oci.New()
goes through the '/var/lib/ig/oci-store' is created and hence locking
start to work as expected.

This PR fixes the issue by ensure '/var/lib/ig/oci-store' exists
before we try to lock.

Signed-off-by: Qasim Sarfraz <qasimsarfraz@microsoft.com>

pkg: Fix printf vet failures surfaced by Go 1.26

Bumping the module go directive to 1.26.0 enables stricter printf/stringintconv
vet analyzers that run as part of `go test`, turning several latent format
mistakes into test build failures. Fix them:

- pkg/container-collection: make EventType.String() a value receiver so
  EventType values (e.g. constants and struct fields) satisfy fmt.Stringer
  and can be formatted with %s.
- pkg/uprobetracer: ProgType is an integer without a String method; format
  it with %d instead of %q.
- pkg/operators/wasm: add the missing idx argument to the parameter-type
  warning, which had one fewer argument than format verbs.
- pkg/operators/ebpf: the logger's Warnf does not support the %w
  error-wrapping verb; use %v.
- pkg/operators/process: use Warnf instead of Warn for a formatted message.

design: GPU telemetry support in Inspektor Gadget

Design proposal for exposing per-device and per-process GPU
telemetry to Inspektor Gadget gadgets, so kernel-side events
(kprobes, uprobes, tracepoints) can be enriched with GPU context
in-kernel via a single BPF map lookup at emit time.

The document defines a stable data-plane contract — four
bpffs-pinned eBPF maps with a versioned schema — and compares three
control-plane alternatives for populating it: a separate writer
process (current prototype), an in-process Go enricher analogous
to the socket enricher, and a WASM operator packaged as an OCI
image. It covers deployment recipes for every IG installation mode
(helm chart DaemonSet, kubectl debug node, local ig binary,
ig-in-container, ig daemon), production deployment mechanics
common to all options (NVIDIA Container Toolkit env vars, library
provisioning, graceful degradation on GPU-less nodes), a non-goals
section listing capabilities that don't fit the snapshot-map model
(event streams, high-frequency sampling, short-lived processes,
DCGM Profiling counters), and open questions for maintainer input.

The recommendation is the separate-writer-process alternative in
its "in-tree, separate image" packaging variant: source in the IG
monorepo at cmd/gpu-ebpf-bridge/, header at
include/gadget/gpu_types.h, published as a distinct container
image alongside the existing IG images, opt-in via a helm chart
value on Kubernetes.

Two proof-of-concept gadgets (gpu_top, gpu_top_per_pid) already
consume the contract and validate the design end-to-end on real

gadgets/snapshot_{process,file}: Read __rcu fields with BPF_CORE_READ

The snapshot_process and snapshot_file gadgets are the only ones that
dereference the __rcu-protected task_struct fields task->cred (and, for
snapshot_process, task->real_parent) directly. On kernels whose BTF carries
the "rcu" btf_type_tag, the verifier tracks such pointers as
"rcu_ptr_or_null_" and rejects a direct dereference:

  program ig_snap_proc: load program: permission denied:
  30: (61) r1 = *(u32 *)(r3 +12): R3 invalid mem access 'rcu_ptr_or_null_'

This is why the gadgets fail to load only on GKE. The "rcu" type tag is
emitted by __rcu (see include/linux/compiler_types.h,
"#define __rcu BTF_TYPE_TAG(rcu)") only when the kernel is built with a
toolchain that supports the attribute, i.e. Clang, together with
CONFIG_PAHOLE_HAS_BTF_TAG. GKE's Container-Optimized OS is Clang-built and
therefore carries the tags and enforces the check, whereas the GCC-built
kernels used on the other CI targets (Ubuntu on the GitHub runners, AKS and
minikube; Amazon Linux on EKS) do not, so the same program loads there.

Read these fields with BPF_CORE_READ(), which goes through
bpf_probe_read_kernel() and is not subject to the RCU pointer check. This
matches how every other gadget and the shared helpers (mntns.h, common.h)
already read these fields, and works on both Clang- and GCC-built kernels.

Relevant kernel changes: 7472d5a642c9 ("compiler_types: define __user as
__attribute__((btf_type_tag("user")))") introduced the btf_type_tag
mechanism, and fca1aa75518c ("bpf: Handle MEM_RCU type properly") added the
verifier enforcement.

pkg/operators/ebpf: Stop lost-samples poller on tracer close

The per-ringbuf-tracer readLostSamples goroutine looped over
`for range ticker.C` with no exit path and never called
ticker.Stop(), so every ringbuf gadget run leaked one goroutine and
one ticker. After the tracer is closed the underlying eBPF collection
is gone, so t.lostSampleMap.Lookup on the closed map keeps failing and
the orphaned goroutine logs "getting lost samples: ..." every second
forever. This is especially harmful for long-lived processes such as
ig daemon and gadgettracermanager that run many gadgets over time.

Add a done channel to Tracer, created in populateTracer. The poller now
defers ticker.Stop() and selects on done before each poll, returning
when the tracer is closed. Tracer.close() closes done.

Signed-off-by: Michael Friese <mfriese@microsoft.com>

localmanager: remove tracer with the id it was registered under

PostGadgetRun removed the tracer using l.subscriptionKey, which is the
key of the container-collection subscription, not the id the tracer was
registered under via AddTracer(). As a result the tracer was never
removed from the tracer-collection, leaking its mount-namespace map and
tracer entry on every gadget run.

legacy handleGadgetInstance path) and use it in PostGadgetRun(), guarding
removal on tracerID instead of mountnsmap.

ebpf: support LIBBPF_PIN_BY_NAME in gadget maps

Pass MapOptions.PinPath = /sys/fs/bpf to cilium/ebpf so that gadget
maps declared with __uint(pinning, LIBBPF_PIN_BY_NAME) can be pinned
to bpffs and reused across gadget invocations.

Previously, libbpf rejected such maps with:

  creating eBPF collection: map <name>: pin by name: missing
  MapOptions.PinPath

This enables three independent use-cases:

  - Persistent state across ig run invocations (a counter map keeps
    its values between runs).

  - Multiple gadgets sharing a map by name.

  - Consumer gadgets reading data produced by an external producer
    process (e.g. a userspace daemon writing telemetry into a
    bpffs-pinned map).

If a pinned map already exists at /sys/fs/bpf/<name>, libbpf reuses
its FD when the spec (type/key_size/value_size/max_entries/flags)
matches; mismatches fail to load with a clear error from cilium/ebpf.

Also document the new behaviour under "Map pinning" in
docs/gadget-devel/gadget-ebpf-api.md.

Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>
Signed-off-by: Alban Crequy <albancrequy@microsoft.com>

ebpf: support iter/bpf_map_elem with GADGET_ITER_TARGET_MAP

Add support for BPF iter programs of type SEC("iter/bpf_map_elem")
so gadgets can read entries from an arbitrary BPF map (including
maps pinned externally) non-destructively. This complements the
existing GADGET_MAPITER, which is destructive (uses
BPF_MAP_LOOKUP_AND_DELETE_BATCH) and restricted to plain HASH maps.

The new macro GADGET_ITER_TARGET_MAP(prog_name, map_name) binds the
iter program to the map whose FD should be passed to bpf_link_create
via iter_info.map_fd. Without this binding, the kernel cannot know
which map a SEC("iter/bpf_map_elem") program is iterating over.

Example:

  struct {
      __uint(type, BPF_MAP_TYPE_LRU_HASH);
      __uint(pinning, LIBBPF_PIN_BY_NAME);
      __type(key,   struct mykey);
      __type(value, struct myval);
      __uint(max_entries, 4096);
  } my_map SEC(".maps");

  GADGET_ITER(my_iter, my_event, dump_my_map);
  GADGET_ITER_TARGET_MAP(dump_my_map, my_map);

  SEC("iter/bpf_map_elem")
  int dump_my_map(struct bpf_iter__bpf_map_elem *ctx) {
      ... bpf_seq_write(ctx->meta->seq, &ev, sizeof(ev));
  }

Implementation:

  - include/gadget/macros.h: add GADGET_ITER_TARGET_MAP macro that
    emits a gadget_mapelem_iter_target_<prog>___<map> variable
    (deliberately distinct stem from gadget_iter_ to avoid the
    prefix-walk in analyze() also matching it as an iterator).

  - pkg/operators/ebpf/types.go: add iterTargetMapPrefix constant.

  - pkg/operators/ebpf/ebpf.go: add iterTargetMaps map to
    ebpfInstance, register the parser in analyze().

  - pkg/operators/ebpf/maps.go: add populateIterTargetMap to parse
    the variable name, validate the program is iter/bpf_map_elem
    and the map exists.

  - pkg/operators/ebpf/attach.go: add case "bpf_map_elem" that
    resolves the bound map and passes its FD via link.IterOptions.

  - pkg/operators/ebpf/iter.go: allow "bpf_map_elem" in
    isIteratorKindSupported so runIterators() actually reads from
    the link.

Tests and docs:

  - gadgets/ci/test_iter_map_elem/: minimal CI gadget that iterates
    an externally-pinned LRU_HASH map and emits one event per entry.
    Registered in gadgets/Makefile.

  - gadgets/ci/test_iter_map_elem/test/integration/: Go integration
    test that pre-creates+pins the map, runs the gadget, asserts the
    emitted JSON matches the inserted entries, and verifies the map
    is unchanged after iteration (non-destructive).

  - docs/gadget-devel/program-types.md: document iter/bpf_map_elem
    and the GADGET_ITER_TARGET_MAP macro under "Iterators".

Ignore node topology labels on managed clusters

On managed Kubernetes clusters (e.g. AKS, GKE) pods carry the well-known
topology labels topology.kubernetes.io/region and topology.kubernetes.io/zone.
They are derived from the node the pod is scheduled on, not from the workload
identity, and they are populated asynchronously. This made several gadget
integration tests flaky on those clusters, through two different code paths.

1. Event matching (test framework)

   Integration tests build their expected event with only the "run" pod label
   (BuildCommonData) and compare captured events with a strict reflect.DeepEqual
   (MatchUnmarshalledEntries). When the topology labels landed before the event
   was captured, the captured podLabels map contained extra keys and the
   comparison failed; otherwise it passed. This affected TestSnapshotProcess,
   TestSnapshotSocket, TestTopTcp, TestContainerFiltering and many others.

   A gadget event should faithfully report the pod's real labels, so this is a
   test-only concern: strip the topology labels in NormalizeCommonData, the
   single normalization helper all gadget integration tests run captured data
   through, so only user-defined labels are compared.

2. Network policy advisor (production)

   The advise_networkpolicy gadget builds pod selectors from the observed pod
   labels and already filters out non-identity labels (controller-revision-hash,
   pod-template-generation, pod-template-hash) via LabelsToIgnore. Emitting the
   topology labels in a NetworkPolicy podSelector is wrong: it pins the policy to
   a region/zone, so once the pod is rescheduled elsewhere the selector no longer
   matches it and the policy silently stops applying. This also made
   TestAdviseNetworkpolicyGadget flaky on managed clusters.

   Add the topology labels, and the deprecated failure-domain.beta.kubernetes.io
   equivalents, to the default ignore list. Both the Kubernetes and Cilium policy
   generators share labelFilter(), so this covers both.

Add unit tests for both changes.

pkg/testing: Gate StartAndStop tests on readiness

StartAndStop gadget tests used fixed sleeps as a proxy for the gadget being
attached and capturing. A slow first-run image pull or program load could
outlive that sleep, causing the workload event to happen before capture began
and leaving an empty output.

Run these gadgets with verbose logging and observe stderr for the existing
"running..." message emitted after operators start. For kubectl-gadget, count
the client-side per-node dispatch messages and wait for a forwarded readiness
message from each target; local ig waits for the bare readiness message. Tests
can opt out when a gadget has a different lifecycle, as ci/stacks does.

Also track the child process exit while waiting so image, signature, verifier,
or capability failures fail immediately rather than waiting for the readiness
timeout. Preserve the original command lifecycle for callers that do not opt
into exit tracking.

Remove the fixed attach-proxy sleeps from the affected integration tests.

Copilot-Session: 4fb111fd-029c-4ade-a9b1-43dd5759c98e

pkg/testing: Filter readiness debug logs

The readiness gate enables verbose logging so it can observe the existing
"running..." debug message. Gadget tests run with go test -v, and Command.Stop
logs the stored stderr even for successful tests, so retaining every debug line
adds hundreds of lines per gadget run to CI output.

Add an optional stderr storage filter. The live observer still sees every line,
while logrus debug lines are omitted from the stored stderr printed by the test
harness. Warnings and errors remain available for validation and diagnostics.

pkg,gadgets: Support OTel stacks from perf_event gadgets

OTel eBPF Profiler symbolization (which produces interpreted-language
frames, notably Python) previously worked only for kprobe/uprobe gadgets.
The correlation id is computed by an OTel entry program reached via
bpf_tail_call, and tail calls require the caller and callee to share the
same BPF_PROG_TYPE. Perf_event gadgets (most importantly profile_cpu,
SEC("perf_event/profiler")) could therefore never get OTel/Python stacks.

Add a perf_event-typed OTel path in parallel to the kprobe one:

- Expose the fork's perf_event entry program via GetPerfEntryEbpfProgram()
  (go.mod bumped to the fork commit that adds the getter) and surface it as
  OtelEbpfProgramPerf alongside the new otel_tc_perf prog-array constant.
- user_stack_map.h now defines both otel_tc_kprobe and otel_tc_perf
  prog-arrays and provides per-program-type wrappers
  (gadget_get_user_stack_from_kprobe() and
  gadget_get_user_stack_from_perf_event()), sharing the ustack fill body in
  __gadget_fill_user_stack(). A given prog-array is only referenced by a
  wrapper of its matching program type, so the kernel prog-array type lock
  is never violated.
- The eBPF loader loads each OTel entry program only into the prog-array
  actually referenced by a gadget program of the matching type, and warns
  (instead of failing) when a mismatched-type program references an array.

Keep gadget_get_user_stack() as the single API most gadgets call: it is now
a _Generic macro that dispatches on the static C type of ctx at compile
time (struct bpf_perf_event_data * -> perf_event, struct pt_regs * ->
kprobe/uprobe). Only the selected wrapper's bpf_tail_call survives, so each
program still references only its own prog-array. There is deliberately no
default association, so an unsupported ctx type is a compile-time error.

Add gadget_get_user_stack_from_tracepoint() for tracepoint gadgets, whose
program type cannot tail-call into any OTel entry program. It always
collects the plain user stack (still symbolizable by the symbol-table
symbolizer) and guards the unsupported OTel path with bpf_core_unreachable():
when --collect-otel-stack is unset (the default) the verifier prunes the
branch at zero cost, and when it is explicitly requested the loader rejects
the program loudly instead of silently returning empty OTel stacks.

Update all callers accordingly: profile_cpu uses the perf_event variant via
gadget_get_user_stack(); audit_seccomp, profile_cuda, trace_capabilities,
trace_malloc and ci/stacks use the kprobe variant via gadget_get_user_stack();
trace_open uses gadget_get_user_stack_from_tracepoint().

gadgets/profile_cpu: Aggregate identical stacks instead of one row per sample

profile_cpu embedded the whole struct gadget_user_stack in the aggregation
key (struct key_t). That struct carries per-sample fields set by
gadget_get_user_stack() - most notably boot_timestamp (bpf_ktime_get_boot_ns)
and otel_correlation_id - so every perf sample produced a unique key. The
map therefore never aggregated: each sample became its own count-1 entry.

With --collect-ustack this yields thousands of samples:1 rows and a bloated,
mis-weighted flamegraph, and it can overflow the map / make the shutdown
flush so large that it gets dropped. The bug is independent of OTel and
affects native symbol-table stacks too.

Fix it the same way profile_cuda does: key only on the stack *identity* (the
user stack id, plus the kernel stack id, kernel ip and process), and move the
full struct gadget_user_stack into the value. The first sample of a given
stack stores the metadata; subsequent identical stacks only bump samples via
__sync_fetch_and_add. The user stack and value struct are fetched into
per-CPU scratch maps to keep them off the 512-byte BPF stack.

The output schema is unchanged: user_stack_raw stays at the same flattened
path (it just moves from key to value), and the new user_stack_id scalar is
hidden from output via json.skip / columns.hidden. Consumers (JSON,
otel-profiles/Pyroscope, IG Desktop) are unaffected; the otel-profiles
exporter uses samples as the per-stack weight, so aggregation preserves
flamegraph weights.

gadgets/trace_exec: Report the device number of the controlling terminal

The tty field is read from tty->index, which is the index of the terminal
within its own driver, not an identifier of the terminal. Two consequences
make the field hard to use:

- The index is only unique per driver, so it is meaningless without knowing
  which driver the terminal belongs to: /dev/pts/0, /dev/tty0 and /dev/ttyS0
  are all reported as 0.
- 0 is also the value reported for a process that has no controlling
  terminal at all, because the chained read through a NULL tty pointer
  yields 0. A process on /dev/pts/0 is therefore indistinguishable from a
  process with no terminal, even though the field is documented as "0 for
  processes without a terminal".

Add tty_major and tty_minor with the device number of the controlling
terminal, computed the same way as the kernel's tty_devnum(), and left at 0:0
when the process has no controlling terminal. This makes the driver explicit
(major 136 for a pseudo terminal, 4 for a virtual console, ...) and gives
consumers a way to tell "no terminal" apart from the first terminal of a
driver.

The tty field is kept as is to avoid breaking existing consumers, and its
description is corrected to say what it actually contains.

Fixes: d2d6a32941cd ("Add tty field")

Docs-exempt: field documentation lives in gadget.yaml, which this commit updates
Signed-off-by: Ben <ben@armosec.io>

symbolizer/otel: handle buffer size for trace_event

The OTel profiler sized the per-CPU trace_events perf buffer to a single
page (~4 KiB) because we passed SamplesPerSecond=0. Under bursty gadgets
(e.g. profile_cuda tracing a GIL-bound process whose uprobes fire many
stacks back-to-back) the buffer overflows and the kernel drops traces
before userspace drains it, so they never reach correlationMap and
Resolve() times out with "no frames found". Set SamplesPerSecond to 20 to
enlarge the buffer (~494 KiB per CPU) and absorb these bursts, and document
why the value is needed even though we do not use CPU sampling

Signed-off-by: Qasim Sarfraz <qasimsarfraz@microsoft.com>

charts: Add DAC_READ_SEARCH  capability

The OTel eBPF profiler reads the ELF files of profiled processes via
/proc/$pid/map_files/*, which go through a ptrace-mode fs-creds check
against the target process. Without DAC_READ_SEARCH the profiler cannot
read libraries of processes running as a different non-root user (e.g. Ray
workers as uid 1000), leaving their stack deltas unloaded and breaking
symbolization. Grant the capability in both the Helm chart and the static
deploy manifest.

include/gadget: add gpu_types.h + gpu_bridge_maps.h public headers

Add the public interface, under include/gadget/, for the four
bpffs-pinned BPF maps that the gpu-ebpf-bridge daemon
(cmd/gpu-ebpf-bridge, added in subsequent commits) publishes:

  gpu_meta                ARRAY[1]   -> struct gpu_meta
  gpu_device              ARRAY[16]  -> struct gpu_device_metrics
  gpu_per_pid             LRU_HASH   -> struct gpu_pid_metrics_aggregated
  gpu_per_pid_per_device  LRU_HASH   -> struct gpu_pid_metrics

Two headers are added:

  gpu_types.h        The map value schema: the four struct layouts
                     plus a GPU_SCHEMA_VERSION. Struct layouts follow
                     BPF CO-RE conventions; consumers detect
                     incompatible changes via GPU_SCHEMA_VERSION and
                     rely on bpf_core_field_exists() for
                     forward-compatible field additions rather than
                     version comparisons.

  gpu_bridge_maps.h  The single source of truth for the map
                     declarations themselves. Both the bridge's own
                     map-defining object and every consumer gadget
                     (gpu_top, gpu_top_per_pid, trace_gpu_starvation,
                     profile_cpu) need identical
                     __uint(pinning, LIBBPF_PIN_BY_NAME) declarations;
                     a consumer selects only the maps it uses via the
                     GPU_BRIDGE_WANT_* macros so it does not pin maps
                     it does not need. Keeping the declarations here
                     stops them being copy-pasted (and drifting)
                     across consumers.

Placing both under include/gadget/ makes them available to consumer
gadgets via the standard gadget include path, so a consumer picks up
the bridge's pinned map instances at load time.

Naming is deliberately vendor-neutral (gpu_*, not nvml_*) so a
future AMD ROCm or Intel oneAPI writer can publish the same map
names and let consumers work unchanged across vendors.

See docs/design/004-gpu-telemetry-enricher.md for the full design.

pkg/gpu-ebpf-bridge/maps: BPF object + Go API for the four pinned bridge maps

Introduces the maps package that owns the four bpffs-pinned BPF
maps published by gpu-ebpf-bridge:

  /sys/fs/bpf/gpu_meta
  /sys/fs/bpf/gpu_device
  /sys/fs/bpf/gpu_per_pid
  /sys/fs/bpf/gpu_per_pid_per_device

Layout:

  bpf/gpu_types.bpf.c            programless BPF object that declares
                                 the four maps with LIBBPF_PIN_BY_NAME.
                                 Loaded via bpf2go so the maps arrive
                                 in the kernel with proper BTF for
                                 the four struct types.
  gen.go                         bpf2go //go:generate directive
                                 following the same TARGET/CFLAGS
                                 pattern as pkg/socketenricher.
  gputypes_{x86,arm64}_bpfel.{go,o}
                                 bpf2go-generated bindings + objects.
  maps.go                        public Bridge type: Open (load+pin),
                                 UpdateMeta/Device/PerPid/PerPidPerDevice,
                                 Delete*, Close (FDs only), Unpin
                                 (bpffs entries).
  types.go                       public type aliases (Meta,
                                 DeviceMetrics, PidMetrics,
                                 PidMetricsAggregated) + constants
                                 mirroring include/gadget/gpu_types.h.
  maps_test.go                   4 unit tests: create+pin, write/read
                                 each map through independent
                                 LoadPinnedMap, reuse across Open,
                                 Unpin idempotent. Require root
                                 (bpffs pin ops).

The Close()/Unpin() split is deliberate: Close releases this
process's file descriptors but leaves the pinned maps in place so
consumer BPF programs can keep reading. Unpin removes the bpffs
entries; only called at clean bridge shutdown when no consumers
are expected to outlive the bridge.

Also adjusts Makefile.btfgen: BPF_ALL_O_FILES now filters the pkg/
objects by presence of a .BTF.ext ELF section instead of taking all of
them. bpftool gen min_core_btf needs the CO-RE relocation records in
.BTF.ext, which clang only emits for objects that contain BPF programs
doing CO-RE reads. This map-only object has none, so without the filter
btfgen fails with "section .BTF.ext not found". Filtering by section
presence rather than by path keeps it working for any future map-only
bpf2go package under pkg/.

and the main gpu-ebpf-bridge binary that drives this package.

pkg/gpu-ebpf-bridge/poller: main bridge loop

Ticker-driven loop that every PollInterval asks the nvml.Poller for
the current device snapshot and per-PID samples, then writes the
results into the four bpffs-pinned maps (via the maps.Bridge from
the previous commit). Writes gpu_meta last so consumers gating
enrichment on last_update_ns see the data before the freshness
signal is refreshed.

Handles three subtleties in NVML's per-PID output that surfaced
during end-to-end validation on an NVIDIA A100 (driver 545 /
Linux 6.17):

  1. Filters pid 0. NVML's nvmlDeviceGetProcessUtilization
     returns 'pid 0' as the bucket for work it cannot attribute to
     a specific userspace process (driver/firmware-internal kernel
     launches). Emitting this into gpu_per_pid would let consumers
     wrongly enrich kernel-init-side eBPF events with nonsensical
     GPU stats.

  2. Folds duplicate (pid, dev) samples within a single tick.
     NVML's rolling-window API typically returns the same
     (pid, dev) tuple multiple times per tick with varying
     utilization values; the aggregator takes the max over each
     utilization field, so consumers see the busiest moment in
     the window rather than an arbitrary last-write-wins pick.

  3. DeviceCount reports distinct devices, not sample count.
     Previously the aggregator incremented per sample, which
     inflated the count wildly for noisy PIDs (observed:
     DeviceCount=72 on a single-GPU host).

poller_test.go includes both a mock-source end-to-end test and a
regression test with a deliberately noisy fake nvml source that
exercises all three of the above.

charts/gadget: opt-in gpu-ebpf-bridge sidecar via bridges.gpu.enabled

Adds a new `bridges.gpu:` values block that, when enabled, injects a
gpu-ebpf-bridge sidecar container into the IG DaemonSet pod. Off
by default.

Three access modes are supported to cover the range of GPU
deployment models seen in production:

  toolkit-env    (default, recommended for most clusters) Sets
                 NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=all +
                 NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES=utility on the sidecar.
                 The NVIDIA Container Toolkit prestart hook then
                 bind-mounts libnvidia-ml.so.1 and grants
                 /dev/nvidia* access without reserving a GPU
                 (same mechanism DCGM Exporter uses). Works on
                 GKE, OpenShift, self-managed k8s with the NVIDIA
                 GPU Operator, and AKS clusters where the GPU
                 Operator is installed.

  hostpath       Bypasses the toolkit hook. Bind-mounts the host's
                 /dev at /host/dev and /usr at /host/usr (readonly)
                 into the sidecar. Both source paths exist on every
                 Linux node, so kubelet accepts the pod regardless
                 of whether an NVIDIA driver is installed. The
                 bridge itself creates /dev/nvidia* symlinks at
                 startup via --symlink-nvidia-devs, and
                 LD_LIBRARY_PATH lists candidate distro-specific
                 driver library paths under /host/usr/. Works on
                 any cluster including AKS default GPU pools where
                 the toolkit-env approach fails because the
                 nvidia-device-plugin denies non-requesting pods.

  device-plugin  Sets resources.limits.nvidia.com/gpu: 1 on the
                 sidecar. WARNING: reserves a full GPU per node,
                 unavailable to workloads. Not recommended for
                 fleet-wide telemetry; only useful with MIG
                 partitioning.

The sidecar is passed --idle-if-no-gpu unconditionally, so on
mixed clusters the DaemonSet keeps running on non-GPU nodes with
the bridge in a healthy Running-but-idle state (no
CrashLoopBackOff). Consequently the chart does not add any
gpu-specific nodeSelector; users who want to restrict IG (and the
bridge) to GPU nodes set the top-level .Values.nodeSelector
themselves.

The sidecar mounts the same /sys/fs/bpf as the main gadget
container, so the bridge's four bpffs-pinned maps are directly
visible to consumer gadgets. No changes to the main gadget
container are required.

Verified with helm template + helm lint against all three
accessMode values; no changes to the default rendering when
bridges.gpu.enabled=false.

See docs/design/004-gpu-telemetry-enricher.md for the full design
including per-mode discussion of the deployment tradeoffs.

gadgets: add gpu_top gadget consuming gpu-ebpf-bridge maps

gpu_top is a user-facing gadget that consumes the bpffs-pinned
'gpu_device' ARRAY map published by the gpu-ebpf-bridge daemon
introduced in the preceding commits of this branch (see
cmd/gpu-ebpf-bridge/ and docs/design/004-gpu-telemetry-enricher.md),
demonstrating end-to-end use of LIBBPF_PIN_BY_NAME and
SEC("iter/bpf_map_elem") (the two new IG capabilities added by the
alban_map_pinning_and_iter commits stacked underneath).

The gadget declares 'gpu_device' with LIBBPF_PIN_BY_NAME, which causes
IG to reuse the externally-pinned map instead of creating a fresh one,
and attaches an iter program to it via GADGET_ITER_TARGET_MAP. Each
run emits one event per active GPU (slots with timestamp_ns == 0 are
filtered out so unused ARRAY entries don't appear in the output).
Iteration is non-destructive, so the gadget can be re-run to refresh
the view without touching the bridge's state.

The 22 telemetry fields cover utilization (SM, memory, video
encoder/decoder), capacity and usage (memory total/used/reserved),
thermals (temperature, power, fan), clocks (SM, memory),
interconnect (PCIe, NVLink), and reliability (ECC, throttle reasons,
compute mode). Less-used fields are hidden by default in gadget.yaml
via columns.hidden and can be shown with --fields. The gadget
refreshes once a second and clears the screen between refreshes
for a top-style live view; memory columns are rendered in
human-readable units (GiB / MiB) rather than raw bytes.

Includes an integration test that mocks the bridge daemon by
pre-creating and pinning gpu_device with realistic A100-class
telemetry. The test validates that only populated slots are emitted,
all fields are correctly propagated, and the map is unchanged after
the iter run.

Requires the gpu-ebpf-bridge daemon to be running on the host or
alongside IG in the DaemonSet (see the helm chart's gpu.enabled
value): the gadget intentionally fails to load if
/sys/fs/bpf/gpu_device does not exist, which is the correct
behaviour (no bridge -> no data).

gadgets: add gpu_top_per_pid gadget with iter/task join

Companion to gpu_top. Where gpu_top iterates the bridge's per-device
ARRAY map, this iterates all live tasks in the kernel via
SEC("iter/task") and, for main threads whose tgid appears in the
bridge's per-PID LRU_HASH map (gpu_per_pid), emits one event with
comm, mntns_id, container/pod/K8s enrichment, and GPU stats
(aggregated across all devices).

The single BPF program is SEC("iter/task"). For each task the program:

  1. Skips threads (pid != tgid) and the swapper (tgid == 0).
  2. Looks up gpu_per_pid[tgid]. Skips if absent or used memory is 0
     (defense in depth; bridge already filters).
  3. Reads task->tgid, ->pid, ->comm, ->cred, ->real_parent->comm/pid
     and ->nsproxy->mnt_ns->ns.inum via BPF_CORE_READ chains, fills
     a standard gadget_process so IG's container, pod, and K8s
     enrichers add runtime context automatically from mntns_id.
  4. Copies the GPU stats and emits via bpf_seq_write.

An earlier revision iterated gpu_per_pid directly via
SEC("iter/bpf_map_elem") and resolved the task with the kfunc
bpf_task_from_pid, but that kfunc is Linux 6.2+ (commit 3f0e6f2b41d3,
2022-11-22), and real deployment targets we care about — including
AKS default GPU node pools on Ubuntu 22.04, kernel 5.15 — do not yet
carry it. Walking the task iterator is a few thousand PIDs at most
per invocation and short-circuits quickly on the
bpf_map_lookup_elem, so the cost is negligible. Requires kernel 5.8+
for iter/task.

Includes an integration test that pre-creates and pins gpu_per_pid
with an entry keyed by the test runner's own PID and a sentinel
never-existing PID. Asserts the gadget emits the real PID with the
host mntns_id (cross-checked against /proc/self/ns/mnt) and skips
the ghost PID, and that the map is unchanged after the iter run.
