pkg/operators/ebpf: Don't pin map/ksym iterators in pod pidns

runIterators() only distinguished per-netns iterators from everything
else, funneling namespace-agnostic iterators (bpf_map_elem, ksym)
through bpfiterns.Read(). When Inspektor Gadget runs inside a pod that
is not in the host pid namespace, that path pins the iterator on the
host bpffs and reads it from a systemd service on the host. This
mechanism only makes sense for task iterators, which need to enumerate
the host's processes.

Map and ksym iterators return the same data regardless of the pid or
network namespace, so pinning is both unnecessary and, in nested
container environments (e.g. minikube with the docker driver), can fail
with "pinning iterator: invalid argument".

Classify iterators three ways instead:
- per-netns (tcp, udp): run per network namespace with setns
- per-pidns (task, task_file): read via the host pid namespace
- namespace-agnostic (bpf_map_elem, ksym): read directly with
  ReadOnCurrentPidNs, without any setns or pinning

This fixes the gpu_top and gpu_top_per_pid iterators, which use
iter/bpf_map_elem.

gadgets/trace_gpu_starvation: add finish_task_switch GPU-starvation tracer

Add a new gadget that detects GPU starvation: a process holds GPU
memory but its GPU sits idle while one of its threads keeps burning
CPU, which is the signature of a pipeline that is CPU-bound in the code
path meant to feed the GPU.

The gadget joins two signals:
- the per-process GPU metrics published by the in-repo gpu-ebpf-bridge
  daemon (VRAM held, and which device the process's memory lives on),
  and
- a finish_task_switch scheduler kprobe that measures each thread's
  on-CPU time and captures its user stack.

GPU idleness is derived from a device-level activity latch rather than a
per-process NVML idle signal. A separate sched_switch program
(ig_sched_switch_devlatch) refreshes, on every context switch on any
CPU, the newest CLOCK_BOOTTIME at which each device was seen with
non-zero SM utilization (from the bridge's gpu_device snapshot); a
process's idle duration is then now - last_active[device], attributed
via the device that the process's GPU memory lives on. Device-level SM
utilization (~167ms NVML sampling) is used deliberately in place of the
per-process NVML utilization API, which only samples at ~1s and
intermittently drops a busy process entirely, so it cannot resolve
sub-second GPU-idle stalls. Because idleness comes from the hardware
SM-utilization signal and not from inferring GPU state from CPU
behaviour, the gadget is not fooled by asynchronous CUDA launches. The
device sample's CLOCK_REALTIME timestamp is converted to CLOCK_BOOTTIME
via the bridge's clock_offset_ns. The latch updater is a separate
program so finish_task_switch, which already does kernel + user stack
walks, keeps an independent verifier budget.

A kprobe is used for the starvation program (rather than the
sched_switch tracepoint) so the user stack can be symbolized through
IG's OTel eBPF-profiler integration, which is reachable only from
kprobe-family programs via bpf_tail_call. The stack is captured at
schedule-in (current == incoming task, where the OTel unwind is valid)
and the on-CPU slice is accounted at schedule-out.

finish_task_switch is emitted with a compiler suffix (e.g.
finish_task_switch.isra.0) on most kernels; a WASM gadgetPreStart
module resolves the right symbol from /proc/kallsyms at startup.

Includes gadget.yaml, WASM symbol-resolution module, README.md/.mdx,
and unit + integration tests.

gadgets/profile_cpu: add --gpu-idle-only GPU-starvation profiler

Add an optional --gpu-idle-only filter that turns profile_cpu into a
GPU-starvation profiler. When enabled, a stack sample is only recorded if
the sampled process currently owns GPU memory (per the gpu-ebpf-bridge
gpu_per_pid map) and its primary GPU is underutilized (SM utilization below
--gpu-util-max-pct) at that instant. The flamegraph then shows exactly the
CPU code that runs while the GPU the process paid for sits idle.

Because it is sampling-based, it has no dependence on the bridge poll
interval and therefore also surfaces "many small gaps" starvation (e.g. a
per-frame CPU preprocessing step keeping an inference GPU at ~50% duty
cycle), which the recency-based trace_gpu_starvation gadget cannot detect.

The pinned bridge maps and CO-RE helpers are shared via
<gadget/gpu_bridge_maps.h>. When the filter is off (the default) the maps
are declared but never read, so profile_cpu still loads on hosts without
the bridge. Stacks are symbolized from native symbol tables only; the OTel
unwinder that produces interpreter (Python) stacks is reachable only from
kprobe-family programs, not this perf_event sampler.

gadgets/trace_gpu_starvation: add video-inference demo workload

Add a self-contained demo that reproduces GPU starvation for both the
trace_gpu_starvation and profile_gpu_starvation gadgets.

video_frame_inference.py runs a frame-by-frame ResNet-50 inference loop in
three modes: "bad" (sequential CPU preprocess -> GPU infer, GPU starves
~320ms/frame), "good" (pipelined with a CUDA stream so the GPU stays busy,
the control case), and "threaded" (a prep thread feeds an inference thread
via a queue, producing two distinct stalling stacks). N_FRAMES is
env-configurable and 0 loops forever so the gadget has time to observe it.

All three modes print a periodic timing report (windowed average of the
per-frame CPU preprocessing time and GPU inference time) so the
stall-duration assumptions can be validated directly from the pod logs,
even when looping forever. GPU time uses CUDA events for accuracy (which
also preserves CPU/GPU overlap in the pipelined mode). REPORT_EVERY tunes
the reporting cadence.

Because the workload needs a GPU node, it is packaged as a container: a
Dockerfile (pytorch CUDA base plus torchvision, numpy, headless OpenCV)
and video-frame-inference.yaml with one pod per mode, each requesting a
GPU and looping forever. A README documents build/push/run and how to
watch it with the two gadgets. This lets the demo be exercised from a
clean git clone with simple docker/kubectl commands.

container-hook: process one fanotify event per read()

The fanotify notifier processes events one at a time, looking up and
deleting the matching record in the ebpf ig_fa_records queue before
handling the next event. However go-fanotify wraps the fanotify fd in a
bufio.Reader with the default 4096-byte buffer, so a single read() syscall
could drain up to ~170 events at once (each event is only 24 bytes).

This broke the coherence between the read() loop and the ig_fa_records
queue: many records piled up ahead of the consumer, overflowed the queue,
and caused "lookup record: key does not exist" errors and lost events.
For permission events it also made the kernel install one fd per event
during a single read(), spiking fd usage under container churn.

Size the bufio buffer to exactly one event so each read() picks a single

safeelf: Harden ELF parsing against memory exhaustion attacks

pkg/symbolizer and pkg/uprobetracer parse ELF files coming from
untrusted containers in a privileged process, and both went through
debug/elf's Symbols() and DynamicSymbols(). Those load the whole symbol
table and its string table in memory, so a crafted ELF with a minimal
.symtab but a ~500 MB .strtab exhausts memory in the daemon.

Add a bounded symbol iterator, IterateSymbols, and move both callers to
it. Symbol table entries are streamed and every section read is bounded,
so memory use no longer depends on what the binary declares:

  .symtab/.dynsym  240 MB (maxSymbolCount x elf.Sym64Size)
  .strtab/.dynstr   16 MiB
  symbol name       64 KB
  symbol count      10M

The string table bound is 16 MiB rather than the ~500 MB the attack
needs. Measured on large real-world binaries, .strtab stays far below
it: dockerd 8.8 MiB, ig 8.6 MiB, docker 2.8 MiB, runc 0.6 MiB. dockerd
also has the largest .dynsym seen (216601 entries) and its .dynstr fits.
That leaves roughly 2x headroom over the largest binary observed while
keeping the bound a meaningful mitigation rather than a formality. It
matches the limit opentelemetry-ebpf-profiler applies to ELF string
tables (libpf/pfelf.maxBytesLargeSection).

In pkg/uprobetracer, always pass the file offset to cilium/ebpf via
UprobeOptions.Address. This bypasses cilium/ebpf's own Symbols() and
DynamicSymbols() path, which has the same unbounded behaviour because
they consider ELF inputs trusted so the caller has to avoid the path
itself.

Make Symbols() and DynamicSymbols() return an error instead of keeping
them as bounded wrappers. Bounding the section sizes does not bound what
debug/elf returns: it materializes a []elf.Symbol, measured at ~187
bytes per symbol on dockerd once names and slice growth are counted. At
the 240 MB .symtab bound that is still ~1.7 GB, so a bounded wrapper
would not have closed the hole it appears to close.

They are stubs rather than deletions because File embeds *elf.File and
Go promotes embedded methods: deleting them does not remove Symbols(),
it silently resolves to the unbounded debug/elf implementation and also
loses the panic recovery. Verified on dockerd, where a File with the
methods deleted still compiles and still returns all 307473 symbols.
Removing them for real means un-embedding *elf.File behind accessors,
which is left to the package refactor discussed in review.

The iterator resolves names from a bounded, once-read string table and
streams entries through a bufio.Reader. Resolving each name with its own
ReadAt and reading each entry with another made iterating dockerd take
22.8s against 144ms for debug/elf, a 158x regression and a worse denial
of service than the one being fixed, since maxSymbolCount allows 10M
symbols. A windowed cache would use less memory but degrades back to one
read per symbol when a crafted binary orders its name offsets
adversarially, whereas reading once is O(1) reads regardless of access
pattern. Streaming entries is also what opentelemetry-ebpf-profiler does
in libpf/pfelf.visitSymbolTable. Iterating dockerd is now 108ms against
139ms for debug/elf.

IterateSymbols does not populate the version fields for .dynsym
(HasVersion, VersionIndex, Version, Library), which would require
parsing .gnu.version and .gnu.version_r. No caller uses them.

Verified that IterateSymbols and debug/elf return identical symbols for
.symtab and .dynsym on dockerd, docker, runc, bash, ls and python3, that
a missing section is not an error, that early exit stops iteration, that
the stubs shadow the promoted methods, and that a crafted ELF declaring
an oversized .symtab or .strtab is rejected before any iteration.

container-hook: Only accept runtime exec events from root

The fanotify listener on the container runtime binary accepts
FAN_OPEN_EXEC_PERM events from any process able to execute runc, so an
unprivileged user can inject a fake container into Inspektor Gadget.

  record is 5152 bytes, this also drops that map from ~330 KB to ~5 KB.

  fsnotify_remove_first_event hold group->notification_lock across the

  group. Using an array rather than a hash means storing the context can
  never fail (no -E2BIG on a full map) and that a leftover value, should a

  wedging the map permanently. The kretprobe now matches on the stored

container-hook: close fanotify fd when a watcher goroutine stops on error

When watchRuntimeBinary or watchPendingContainers hit an error from
GetEvent(), the goroutine logs it and stops, as before. But it used to
leave the fanotify fd open with its permission marks still active. With no
goroutine left to answer the permission events, every runc exec (for the
runtime-binary group) or every access to a watched pid-file directory (for
the pid-file group) would then block forever in the kernel waiting for a
response, freezing container lifecycle host-wide.

Close the fanotify fd of the failing watcher before it returns. Closing the
fd makes the kernel drop our marks and auto-resolve any pending or future
permission events, so the failure degrades from a host-wide freeze to a
loss of container detection. Close() may also close the same fd later, but
os.File.Close() is idempotent and its internal fdMutex makes concurrent
closes safe, closing the underlying fd at most once.

The runtimeBinaryNotify group is read-only after startup (its mark is set
once in install()), so closing it from its reader is trivially safe. The
pidFileDirNotify group is different: the runtime goroutine keeps adding and
removing marks on it via monitorRuntimeInstance() while the pid-file reader
runs, so closing that fd from the reader could race a mark from the runtime
goroutine. That matters because go-fanotify's Mark calls fanotify_mark(2)
on the raw int fd, bypassing the os.File protection: once the fd is closed
its number can be reused by another fanotify user in the same process (IG
can be embedded as a library), and a stale mark would then corrupt an
unrelated fanotify group.

Guard it with pidMarkMu + pidNotifyClosed: pidMark() and pidClose() take
the mutex, and pidMark() skips the syscall once the fd is closed, so no
mark is ever issued on a closed/reused fd. The read (GetEvent) and response
paths are deliberately left outside the mutex: they go through the os.File,
whose internal/poll layer refcounts the fd and flips a closed flag on
Close, so a read in flight defers the real close and a read after Close
fails cleanly without touching a reused number. Keeping them lock-free is
required because the read blocks legitimately and must remain interruptible
by pidClose().

This reduces the damage of an unexpected error; retrying transient errors
(ENOMEM/EMFILE) instead of stopping is left for future work.

pkg/container-hook: Add FAN_MARK_IGNORED_SURV_MODIFY to ignore marks

The ignore marks we add on config.json and on passwd/log.json/runtime are
frequently not created at all, and fanotify_mark(2) reports no error when
that happens.

fanotify_add_inode_mark() bails out early when the inode is open for write
by any task, unless the ignore mask is meant to survive modification
(fs/notify/fanotify/fanotify_user.c):

	if ((flags & FANOTIFY_MARK_IGNORE_BITS) &&
	    !(flags & FAN_MARK_IGNORED_SURV_MODIFY) &&
	    inode_is_open_for_write(inode))
		return 0;

The container runtime writes these files immediately before we mark them.
Even though it closes its descriptor first, a fork() elsewhere in the
runtime duplicates the still-open write descriptor into the child, and the
child only drops it at execve(). i_writecount therefore stays elevated for
several milliseconds after the runtime's own close(), and a mark issued in
that window is silently dropped.

This was observed on a Kubernetes node: containerd opened config.json,
forked while it was open, and closed its own descriptor 3.9ms later, but
the inode stayed writable for a further 31.7ms until the forked child
reached execve(). The ignore mark was requested 15.1ms into that window and
never created. Reads of config.json by runc then generated FAN_ACCESS_PERM
events that the ignore mark was supposed to suppress.

FAN_MARK_IGNORED_SURV_MODIFY exempts us from that bailout, and additionally
keeps the ignore mask from being cleared by later writes to the file. It has
been available since fanotify was introduced in 2.6.37, so it needs no
kernel version guard.

pkg/container-collection: Replace nodes/proxy by nodes/configz.

Since cd40f60ac959 ("container-collection/k8s: auto detect container runtime socket path"),
Inspektor Gadget relies on nodes/proxy to access to configz to get the container
runtime socket path.
Unfortunately, nodes/proxy, even with the "get" verb permits remote code
execution [1].
With k8s 1.36, fine-grained kubelet API authorizations were graduated to
stable to only have [2]. One of these permits accessing configz.
Unfortunately, dialoging with the kubelet is not as easy as dialog with the API
server. Particularly, this uses HTTP and requires the kubelet certificate to be
provided.

This commits permits replaces nodes/proxy with nodes/configz. The kubelet
certificate is fetched, at runtime, through insecure TLS by dialing the node
kubelet. This way, communications remain local and reduces risks of MITM
attacks.

uprobetracer: Add note iteration cap to USDT parsing

Add maxNoteCount (10,000) limit to prevent CPU denial of service from a
crafted .note.stapsdt section containing millions of tiny valid notes.

While individual note allocations are already bounded by maxNoteFieldSize
(1 MB), there was no cap on the total number of iterations. A crafted
ELF could have a large section with millions of minimal notes (~44 bytes
each), causing sustained CPU burn in the privileged IG process.

symbolizer/debuginfod: Add file size check before parsing

Check debuginfo file size against MaxExecutableSize (512 MB) before
calling NewSymbolTableFromFile(). Without this check, an oversized
debuginfo file from a compromised debuginfod server or cache corruption
would bypass the size check that exists in the normal symbolizer path
(symtab.go:180) and hit the same parsing code.

Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>
Signed-off-by: Alban Crequy <albancrequy@microsoft.com>

safeelf: Harden ELF parsing against memory exhaustion attacks

pkg/symbolizer and pkg/uprobetracer parse ELF files coming from
untrusted containers in a privileged process, and both went through
debug/elf's Symbols() and DynamicSymbols(). Those load the whole symbol
table and its string table in memory, so a crafted ELF with a minimal
.symtab but a ~500 MB .strtab exhausts memory in the daemon.

Add a bounded symbol iterator, IterateSymbols, and move both callers to
it. Symbol table entries are streamed and every section read is bounded,
so memory use no longer depends on what the binary declares:

  .symtab/.dynsym  240 MB (maxSymbolCount x elf.Sym64Size)
  .strtab/.dynstr   16 MiB
  symbol name       64 KB
  symbol count      10M

The string table bound is 16 MiB rather than the ~500 MB the attack
needs. Measured on large real-world binaries, .strtab stays far below
it: dockerd 8.8 MiB, ig 8.6 MiB, docker 2.8 MiB, runc 0.6 MiB. dockerd
also has the largest .dynsym seen (216601 entries) and its .dynstr fits.
That leaves roughly 2x headroom over the largest binary observed while
keeping the bound a meaningful mitigation rather than a formality. It
matches the limit opentelemetry-ebpf-profiler applies to ELF string
tables (libpf/pfelf.maxBytesLargeSection).

In pkg/uprobetracer, always pass the file offset to cilium/ebpf via
UprobeOptions.Address. This bypasses cilium/ebpf's own Symbols() and
DynamicSymbols() path, which has the same unbounded behaviour because
they consider ELF inputs trusted so the caller has to avoid the path
itself.

Make Symbols() and DynamicSymbols() return an error instead of keeping
them as bounded wrappers. Bounding the section sizes does not bound what
debug/elf returns: it materializes a []elf.Symbol, measured at ~187
bytes per symbol on dockerd once names and slice growth are counted. At
the 240 MB .symtab bound that is still ~1.7 GB, so a bounded wrapper
would not have closed the hole it appears to close.

They are stubs rather than deletions because File embeds *elf.File and
Go promotes embedded methods: deleting them does not remove Symbols(),
it silently resolves to the unbounded debug/elf implementation and also
loses the panic recovery. Verified on dockerd, where a File with the
methods deleted still compiles and still returns all 307473 symbols.
Removing them for real means un-embedding *elf.File behind accessors,
which is left to the package refactor discussed in review.

The iterator resolves names from a bounded, once-read string table and
streams entries through a bufio.Reader. Resolving each name with its own
ReadAt and reading each entry with another made iterating dockerd take
22.8s against 144ms for debug/elf, a 158x regression and a worse denial
of service than the one being fixed, since maxSymbolCount allows 10M
symbols. A windowed cache would use less memory but degrades back to one
read per symbol when a crafted binary orders its name offsets
adversarially, whereas reading once is O(1) reads regardless of access
pattern. Streaming entries is also what opentelemetry-ebpf-profiler does
in libpf/pfelf.visitSymbolTable. Iterating dockerd is now 108ms against
139ms for debug/elf.

IterateSymbols does not populate the version fields for .dynsym
(HasVersion, VersionIndex, Version, Library), which would require
parsing .gnu.version and .gnu.version_r. No caller uses them.

Verified that IterateSymbols and debug/elf return identical symbols for
.symtab and .dynsym on dockerd, docker, runc, bash, ls and python3, that
a missing section is not an error, that early exit stops iteration, that
the stubs shadow the promoted methods, and that a crafted ELF declaring
an oversized .symtab or .strtab is rejected before any iteration.

container-hook: Only accept runtime exec events from root

The fanotify listener on the container runtime binary accepts
FAN_OPEN_EXEC_PERM events from any process able to execute runc, so an
unprivileged user can inject a fake container into Inspektor Gadget.

Record the euid of the caller in the ebpf program and ignore the events
from a non-root caller. euid is read as a kuid_t, so it is relative to
the initial user namespace: a user mapped to uid 0 in a user namespace
is not seen as root.

Rootless containers are not supported by the container hook.

types: Validate container IDs

Container IDs come from untrusted sources such as the runc command line
or a bundle directory. They end up in logs, file paths and runtime
metadata, so an attacker can use them for log injection or path
traversal.

Add types.ValidateContainerID() and reject invalid IDs in the container
collection, in the container hook and in ParseContainerID().

The accepted format is the one used by runc's validateID(): a non-empty
string of [A-Za-z0-9_+-.] that is usable as a file name. The OCI
runtime-spec does not define a character set, so use the same rules as
the runtime creating the container.

uprobetracer: Support selected stripped Go binaries

When attaching a uprobe and the symbol is not found in the standard
ELF symbol table, resolve it from Go's .gopclntab metadata.

Resolving a function address from .gopclntab requires the base address
of the Go text segment. It is looked up in the following order:

- moduledata.text from the .go.module section. Go 1.26 moved moduledata
  to its own section (Go commit 9f5cd43fe612) and stopped storing the
  text start in the pclntab header (Go commit 0e1bd8b5f17e), so this is
  the only reliable source for those binaries.
- pcHeader.textStart, for binaries built with older Go versions.
- the runtime.text symbol or the internally linked .text layout.

Externally linked stripped binaries without pclntab textStart or
runtime.text are rejected rather than resolved with an unsafe .text.Addr
guess. Binaries whose pclntab is present only in PT_LOAD data after
section headers are removed are not supported.

The resolved virtual address is converted to a file offset using the
executable LOAD segments. Use the panic-safe ELF parser and reject
overflowing virtual-address to file-offset conversions.

Signed-off-by: Alban Crequy <albancrequy@microsoft.com>

ci/uprobe: Add Go integration test

Add a CI-only gadget attaching uprobes to a "main.target" Go function in
several Go binaries shipped in a locally built test image, to check that
uprobe symbol resolution keeps working for Go binaries built with
different Go versions and different linking and stripping options.

The workload image contains the same program built with Go 1.25 and
Go 1.26, each in a normal, PIE, linker-stripped (-ldflags='-s -w') and
strip(1)-ed variant. A single builder stage is used and the additional
Go toolchains are fetched through GOTOOLCHAIN, so only one golang image
is pulled. The image is built by "make -C gadgets ci/uprobe/workload-image"
and is not pushed anywhere; the mechanism is generic and picks up any
ci/<gadget>/workload/Dockerfile.

The test only runs with the docker runtime: the workload image is only
available to the local Docker daemon and what is tested here does not
depend on the container runtime.

The gadget generates one uprobe section per binary through C macros, so
a single gadget and a single short-lived container cover all variants.

Since the workload image is built locally instead of being pulled, add an
opt-in WithoutImagePull() option to the container test helpers. Existing
tests keep pulling their image by default.

pkg/gadget-service: Report the PID namespace of the gadget service

Some features do not work when Inspektor Gadget does not run in the
initial PID namespace. The OTel eBPF profiler symbolizer is one of them:
eBPF programs report PIDs relative to the initial PID namespace, while
the profiler resolves them through its own /proc, so it silently
symbolizes nothing when the two differ.

The gadget image is distroless, so this cannot be diagnosed by exec'ing
into the pod. Report it in the InfoResponse of GetInfo() instead, and
show it in "kubectl gadget version --details".

Add host.IsInitPidNs() for this. It is stricter than the existing
host.IsHostPidNs(), which compares with PID 1 as seen through HostProcFs:
when the host itself is containerized, for instance a minikube node
started with the docker driver, IsHostPidNs() returns true while the PIDs
reported by eBPF are still unusable. Instead, compare with
PROC_PID_INIT_INO, the inode the kernel statically allocates to the
initial PID namespace.

Both booleans are optional in the protocol so that a check that could not
be performed, or a server too old to report it, is not confused with a
negative answer.

While at it, factor the inode reading out of isHostNamespace().

gadgets/profile_cpu: Run OTel stacks workload in a container

The profile_cpu OTel stack-symbolization test used to run the Python
workload as a local process and was therefore restricted to ig --host
mode, skipping in container and Kubernetes modes.

Now that python:3.13-slim is mirrored to ghcr.io/inspektor-gadget/ci/python
by the dockerhub-mirror workflow, run the workload in a container instead
and drop the IgLocalTestComponent skip, so the test also covers the
container and Kubernetes paths (including container/pod enrichment of the
sampled stacks).

The workload script is written into the container at runtime, with a
shebang resolved from the image (the official Python images ship the
interpreter in /usr/local/bin), so that its comm stays "cpuburn.py" and
can be filtered on. The now-unused workload directory is removed.

The IgLocalTestComponent skip is replaced by a new RequireInitPidNs()
helper that checks the actual causal condition instead of the test
harness: the OTel eBPF profiler symbolizer resolves the PIDs reported by
eBPF programs, which are relative to the initial PID namespace, through
its own /proc, so it symbolizes nothing when Inspektor Gadget itself does
not run in the initial PID namespace. That is the case in Kubernetes,
where the gadget DaemonSet runs with hostPID: false, and on minikube with
the docker driver, where even the node is in a nested PID namespace. Note
that this is about the PID namespace of Inspektor Gadget: the traced
workloads can be anywhere.

When ig is executed by the test it shares its PID namespace, so the check
is done locally. With kubectl-gadget, ig runs in the gadget pod, whose
image is distroless, so the information is retrieved over gRPC with
"kubectl-gadget version --details -o json" instead.

Fixes: a98fd5978865 (".github: Mirror python:3.13-slim image for CI tests")

build: Fix broken .PHONY declarations in Makefiles

Three .PHONY declarations in the root Makefile were misspelled .PHOHY,
and gadgets/Makefile had nine empty '.PHONY:' lines that declare
nothing, so targets like pull, clean, push, and test-unit were never
actually marked phony. A stray file with a target's name then silently
disables it:

    $ touch gadgets/pull && make -C gadgets pull
    make: 'pull' is up to date.

Marking the aggregator targets alone is not enough: push, push-existing,
sign, sign-existing and clean have no recipe of their own, and the work
happens in the %-push, %-sign, %-clean, ... pattern rules, which make
does not allow to be declared phony. A stray file such as
trace_open-clean therefore still skipped that one gadget's step
silently.

Bring over the phony_explicit idiom the root Makefile already uses for
its own implicit rules, and make every action-only pattern rule depend
on it, so the phony attribute is inherited. Also declare the sign and
sign-existing aggregators, which had no declaration at all, and fill in
or drop the remaining empty ones.

Note that make push and make sign remain broken for an unrelated,
pre-existing reason: %-push depends on a %-build pattern rule that has
never existed in this Makefile.

uprobetracer: Fix panic parsing USDT notes of 32-bit ELF files

The stapsdt note parser derives wordSize from the ELF class, but read the
three address fields with ByteOrder.Uint64() regardless. On an ELFCLASS32
file this evaluates to Uint64(desc[:4]): binary.LittleEndian.Uint64 starts
by evaluating b[7], and Go bounds-checks that against the slice length (4)
rather than the capacity, so the parser panics with "index out of range [7]
with length 4".

The desc length guard added in 3f39e27a6a35 does not help, since it is
sized in wordSize units: for a 32-bit file the threshold is 3*4 = 12, so
any note clearing the guard still triggers the over-read. A length guard
sized in wordSize units cannot protect reads performed at a fixed 8-byte
width.

As a result the whole ELFCLASS32 USDT path was unusable: every 32-bit
binary carrying a valid stapsdt note crashed the parser. Because the ELF
may come from an untrusted container and is parsed on a container-attach
goroutine that has no panic recovery, the panic also terminated the
privileged process, dropping monitoring on that node.

Read each address field at the parser's actual word size, and wrap
getUsdtInfo() in defer/recover so a parser panic on attacker-supplied ELF
can never take down the process, as originally intended by 3f39e27a6a35.

Fixes: 7ee5e7a90bbc ("pkg/uprobetracer: support USDT trace points")
Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>
Signed-off-by: Alban Crequy <albancrequy@microsoft.com>

uprobetracer: Bound bytes read from the USDT note section

The .note.stapsdt section may carry SHF_COMPRESSED, in which case
Section.Open() transparently decompresses it, so a small file on disk can
expand to an arbitrary amount of data.

The existing caps do not bound this: maxNoteFieldSize (1 MiB) and
maxNoteCount (10,000) only bound each note individually, and their product
still allows around 10 GB of notes to be read and allocated. Parsing such a
file drove the process to 11.9 GB RSS and got it OOM-killed. Since the ELF
comes from an untrusted container and is parsed in a privileged process,
that terminates gadget monitoring on the node, and the resulting global
memory pressure can take down unrelated processes too. A failed allocation
is a fatal runtime error, so the recover() in getUsdtInfo cannot contain it.

Reject compressed note sections, as pkg/utils/safeelf already does for
symbol and string tables. Nothing legitimate is lost: the section holds a
few KiB of probe descriptors and no toolchain compresses it.

Rejecting is not sufficient on its own though, so also bound the bytes
actually read. For an uncompressed section Open() returns a reader spanning
the rest of the file rather than just the section, and the size declared in
the section header is no use as a bound either: it is attacker-controlled,
and debug/elf does not enforce it when reading through Open(), it only uses
it to seek. Section.Data() does read exactly that many bytes, which is why
the callers in resolveGoSymbol() are already bounded, but the note section
is parsed as a stream and cannot use it.

Fixes: 7ee5e7a90bbc ("pkg/uprobetracer: support USDT trace points")
Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>
Signed-off-by: Alban Crequy <albancrequy@microsoft.com>

uprobetracer: Map USDT probe addresses through PT_LOAD file content only

vaddr2ElfOffset() turns the virtual address of a probe into the file offset
the uprobe is attached to. It walked every program header and matched on
Memsz, which is wrong in three ways.

Memsz covers the memory image, which is larger than the file content for
segments holding .bss. An address in that tail has no bytes in the file, yet
it was still mapped to an offset, pointing the uprobe at unrelated file
content. Match on Filesz instead, which is what actually backs the mapping.

Only PT_LOAD segments describe the memory image, but all types were
considered. Other segments overlap the PT_LOAD ones, so a crafted program
header of another type could be used to redirect the mapping to an arbitrary
file offset. Skip anything that is not PT_LOAD.

Finally prog.Vaddr+prog.Memsz can wrap. This is only reachable on ELFCLASS64,
where both fields are read straight from the file: on ELFCLASS32 they are
widened from 32-bit fields and their sum always fits. Compare the offset
within the segment instead, and check the final addition for overflow too.

The computed offset is passed to the kernel as a uprobe attach address, so
the practical effect is a probe attached to the wrong place or a failed
attach rather than memory unsafety in the parser.
